hook: One machine is easy. What changes when it's 100,000 machines and some of them fail every hour?
title: 100,000 machines turns storage into a different system
body: A storage system on one machine is easy. Spread it over 100,000 machines, many regions and thousands of teams, while machines fail every hour, and every shortcut breaks. Scaling it comes down to three questions. How do you split the data? Where do you put each piece? How do you stay fast and fair as you grow? Splitting is **partitioning**, choosing disks and failure domains is **placement**, and staying fast means taming hot spots, tenants, regions, capacity and tail latency.
takeaway: Split, place, stay fast: every scaling problem lands in one of three buckets.
deeper:
**One app, five data types:** Take a global app with 1 billion users storing profiles, photos and videos, messages, logs and events, and analytics. Each type stresses a different part of the system. Photos and videos pile up into exabytes. Messages burst at peak hours. Thumbnails become trillions of tiny objects. Search, ads and ML want the same clusters. Some users live under laws that keep their data in their region.

**The order matters:**
1. Split data into shards, the basic tool.
2. Place those shards so no single failure destroys every copy and no disk gets too much traffic.
3. Keep it working as load shifts: hot items appear, tenants collide, regions add speed-of-light delay, hardware must be bought months ahead, and fan-out requests wait on the slowest server.

**The catch:** You never finish step 1 and move on. Growth reopens all three questions at once.

quiz.q: Your design review says the new photo service 'must scale'. Which three questions should you force the design to answer?
quiz.a: How the data is split into shards, where each shard's copies are placed (failure domains, heat), and how it stays fast and fair as it grows (hot spots, tenants, regions, capacity, tail latency).

mcq.q: Which trio of questions frames scaling a storage system to 100,000 machines?
options: How to split data, where to place it, how to stay fast and fair
How to compress data, encrypt it, and back it up
Which database, which cloud, and which language to use
How to cache reads, batch writes, and index columns
mcq.why: Scaling is partitioning (split), placement (where copies live), and staying fast and fair under hot spots, tenants, regions, capacity and tail latency.

hook: Two systems both 'scale'. One dies at 10× the bytes, the other at 10× the tenants. How are both true?
title: 'It must scale' hides at least six different problems
body: “The system must scale” sounds like one requirement. It hides at least six, and each breaks a different part. **Capacity** fills disks and stretches rebuild times. IOPS and throughput saturate disk heads, NICs and storage-node CPUs. Metadata operations overload the metadata service, often before any data node. Object count bloats indexes and per-object memory. Tenants create fairness, isolation and quota fights. Regions add latency, consistency and legal limits. Name the growing dimension and you know what breaks first.
takeaway: Never accept “it scales” without asking: scales along which axis?
deeper:
**Mapped to one app:** In a 1-billion-user app, photos and videos reach exabytes, so disks fill and rebuilds grow. Message writes at peak hours hammer heads, NICs and CPUs. Listing a user's photo album is a metadata operation. Trillions of small thumbnails blow up index size, memory per object and directory size. Search, ads and ML share one cluster. EU users' data must stay in the EU.

**Why it's diagnostic:** Each dimension puts a different component on the critical path. A design that absorbs 10× more bytes by adding disks can still collapse at 10× more objects, because the metadata service, not the disks, is the bottleneck there.

**The catch:** Dimensions interact. Bigger drives add capacity but not IOPS. More tenants add bursts that compete for the same IOPS. A capacity plan that tracks only petabytes can look healthy right up to the day it fails on something else.

quiz.q: A colleague's design handles 10× the petabytes by adding disks. Why might it still fail when the object count grows 10×?
quiz.a: Object count stresses a different component: the metadata service, index size and per-object memory. Adding disks scales bytes, not metadata entries.

mcq.q: Which component usually breaks first when metadata operations like listing an album grow?
options: The metadata service, often before data nodes
The disk heads on the data nodes
The cross-region network links
The per-tenant quota system
mcq.why: Metadata operations (opens, lists, renames, lookups) break the metadata service, often before the data nodes are stressed at all.

hook: You swap 4 TB drives for 20 TB drives and get 5× the capacity. Why does your hot data get slower?
title: Bigger drives, same arm: IOPS per terabyte keeps falling
body:
Bytes and operations scale separately. A 20 TB hard drive holds five times the data of a 4 TB drive, but it still has one head arm doing roughly 100-200 **random IOPS** (assuming a typical 7,200 RPM drive). So each terabyte gets a fifth of the random operations. Cold data never notices. Hot data suffers badly, because far more bytes now compete for the same arm.

Capacity grew fivefold. The number of things the drive can do per second did not.
takeaway: Disks grow in bytes, not in arms. Plan IOPS separately from capacity.
deeper:
**Why the arm caps you:** Random performance on a hard drive is set by seek time and rotation, not bit density. Packing more bits under the arm does not make it move faster or the platter come around sooner. So IOPS per drive stays roughly flat while terabytes per drive climb.

**The math:** Take 150 IOPS as a midpoint. On 4 TB that is about 37 IOPS per terabyte. On 20 TB it is 7.5. Same drive count, a fifth of the random capacity per byte.

**Where it bites:** If several hot objects land on one big drive, its small IOPS budget becomes a hot spot, which is why placement must be heat-aware. Hyperscale object stores like S3 spread each tenant thinly across huge numbers of drives. Smaller systems reserve IOPS headroom or move hot data to flash.

**The catch:** A cluster sized only by bytes can have plenty of free space and still fail to serve its traffic.

quiz.q: You move a hot dataset from 4 TB drives to 20 TB drives, keeping the drive count and doubling the data. Free space looks great. Why does latency get worse?
quiz.a: Each drive still does roughly 100-200 random IOPS but now holds twice the hot data, so requests queue on the same arms. Capacity grew; IOPS did not.

mcq.q: Why does IOPS per terabyte fall as hard drives get bigger?
options: Each drive still has one arm with roughly the same random IOPS
Bigger platters spin more slowly to stay cool
Larger drives need more error correction per read
Controllers throttle big drives to extend lifespan
mcq.why: Random IOPS come from one head arm's seeks and rotation, roughly 100-200 for a 7,200 RPM drive, regardless of capacity.

predict.q: A 20 TB drive replaces a 4 TB drive of the same speed class. Random IOPS per terabyte:
options: Falls to about a fifth
Stays about the same
Rises about fivefold

hook: A billion files that fit on one drive can still take down your storage system. What runs out first?
title: One billion 1 KB objects: 1 TB of data, a billion entries
body: Count matters as much as size. One billion 1 KB objects add up to only 1 TB. But they are also one billion **metadata entries**, and each one costs index space, memory, and work every time you list or look something up. Many costs are per object, not per byte. That is why many systems hit the limit of their metadata service long before they run out of disk. HDFS is the famous example.
takeaway: Petabytes fill disks. Object counts fill metadata servers, and those fill first.
deeper:
**Two planes, two limits:** The data plane scales by adding disks. The metadata plane needs consistency and often lives on fewer machines, so a system that easily handles 10× the bytes can still fail at 10× the objects.

**The cautionary tale:** HDFS kept its namespace in one server's memory, so the number of files it could hold was capped by that server, not by the data nodes' free space.

**The running example:** Trillions of small thumbnails are modest in bytes next to full-size videos, yet they could dominate metadata load: index size, memory per object, directory size.

**What scale looks like:** A representative Meta Tectonic cluster in 2021 tracked 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks, with metadata in a sharded key-value store sized for that count. In any design review, ask for the expected object count, not just the expected petabytes.

quiz.q: Team A stores 10 PB of video. Team B stores 50 TB of 1 KB thumbnails. Which is more likely to break the metadata service, and why?
quiz.a: Team B. 50 TB of 1 KB objects is about 50 billion entries, while video is fewer, larger files. Metadata cost scales with count, not bytes.

mcq.q: One billion 1 KB objects total about 1 TB. What usually limits a system storing them?
options: The metadata service tracking a billion entries
The raw disk capacity of the cluster
The network bandwidth to the data nodes
The erasure-coding CPU on storage nodes
mcq.why: Many costs are per object: metadata entries, index memory, listing work. The metadata service hits its limit long before disks fill.

hook: Your data no longer fits on one machine. Every fix you pick must answer the same question. Which one?
title: Sharding's one question: which shard owns this key?
body: When one machine cannot hold or serve all the data, you split it. **Partitioning**, also called **sharding**, cuts a dataset into pieces called shards, and each shard lives on one server or one replica group. That raises one question every sharded system must answer: for a given key, which shard owns it? There are four main answers: range partitioning, hash partitioning, consistent hashing, and directory-based lookup. Each trades scans, even spread, data movement and flexibility differently.
takeaway: Sharding is easy to start. The key-to-shard rule is what you live with.
deeper:
**Four axes to judge by:** How evenly keys spread. Whether range scans stay cheap. How much data moves when capacity changes. How freely you can put a shard where you want.

**The quick map:** Range partitioning keeps sorted keys together: cheap scans, but hot spots. Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly but destroys order, and naive hash mod N moves almost every key when the server count changes. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes limits movement to about 1/N. Directory-based partitioning stores an explicit map, giving total freedom at the price of a critical lookup service.

**They stack:** Real systems combine them. Google's Slicer has applications hash keys into a large key space, then assigns ranges of that hashed space to servers from a central controller.

**Rule of thumb:** Scan-heavy workloads lean to ranges. Point-lookup workloads lean to hashing. Workloads that need placement by load, hardware or region lean to a directory.

quiz.q: A chat app constantly asks for 'all messages in chat X between T1 and T2'. A metrics store does only single-key lookups. Which partitioning family fits each?
quiz.a: The chat app wants range partitioning, which keeps sorted keys together so time scans touch few shards. The lookup-only store can hash for even spread.

mcq.q: Which of these is one of the four main answers to 'which shard owns this key?'
options: Directory-based lookup
Write-ahead logging
Two-phase commit
Log-structured merging
mcq.why: The four are range, hash, consistent hashing and directory-based partitioning. The others are storage or transaction techniques, not key-to-shard rules.

hook: A query wants every message in one chat from 9:00 to 9:05. Why can one scheme answer it from a single shard?
title: Range partitioning: sorted keys make scans cheap
body: Some queries want neighbors: all messages in this chat between T1 and T2. In **range partitioning**, each shard owns a continuous, sorted range of keys, say user IDs a to f on shard 1 and f to m on shard 2. A small table maps ranges to shards, and a range that grows too large is split in two. Because data sorted together stays together, a time-bounded scan touches only one or a few neighboring shards.
takeaway: Store keys in order and a range query becomes a short walk.
deeper:
**Many names, one idea:** Bigtable calls a range a tablet, Spanner a split, HBase a region, CockroachDB a range. The mapping table is small because it stores only boundaries, not individual keys.

**Splits and merges come naturally:** Pick a split key inside an oversized range and create two children. After deletes, Spanner and CockroachDB merge small adjacent ranges back together. Explicit boundaries let the system adapt to uneven growth without rehashing anything.

**The weakness:** Load follows the key distribution. Evenly accessed keys balance well after a few splits. Skewed keys, like timestamps or auto-incrementing IDs, pile all activity onto one end of the key space.

**Scorecard:** Needs splits for even spread. Range scans: yes. Data moved on resize: only the split ranges. Flexibility: medium.

quiz.q: You range-partition a chat store by (chat_id, timestamp). Why does 'last 5 minutes of chat 42' usually hit one server?
quiz.a: Keys are sorted, so chat 42's recent messages are contiguous and fall in one range, or a few adjacent ones, owned by one shard.

mcq.q: What does range partitioning's mapping table store?
options: Range boundaries and the shard owning each
A hash of every key and its server
Every key's exact disk location
A replica count for each individual key
mcq.why: Each shard owns a continuous sorted key range, so the table only needs boundaries per range, which keeps it small.

hook: Twenty servers. One is pinned at 100% and nineteen are idle. The keys are timestamps. What happened?
title: Timestamp keys turn range sharding into a one-server show
body: Range partitioning has one classic trap. If keys are timestamps or increasing IDs, every new key is larger than all existing keys, so every write lands in the last range. One server takes all the writes while the rest sleep. Splitting that range barely helps: the new top range instantly becomes the hot one. The problem is the **key design**, not the shard count, and adding servers only adds more idle servers.
takeaway: An always-increasing key has one hot end, however many shards you add.
deeper:
**Even smart splitters give up:** DynamoDB's 2022 paper says a sequentially accessed key range will not benefit from split-for-consumption, and DynamoDB detects the pattern and skips useless splits. Auto-splitting fixes hot ranges but cannot fix a monotonically increasing key.

**Fix the key, not the partitioner:** Prefix keys with a hash so consecutive writes scatter across the key space, or use randomized IDs instead of counters. Both spread writes across all ranges.

**The trade-off:** You give up some cheap scans. Records written close together in time no longer sit close together, so 'the last hour' now touches many shards. Some designs accept that for write-heavy tables and keep strict order only where scans truly matter.

**The rule:** Range order is a gift to reads that scan and a curse to writes that always append at the same end. Check your write pattern before you choose it.

quiz.q: You split the hot last range of a timestamp-keyed table in two. A minute later one server is hot again. Which one, and why?
quiz.a: The server holding the new top child. Every new timestamp sorts after existing keys, so all writes land in whichever range holds the highest keys.

mcq.q: What fixes the hot spot from timestamp keys in a range-partitioned table?
options: Prefixing keys with a hash or using random IDs
Splitting the last range more aggressively
Adding more servers to the cluster
Raising the per-shard write quota
mcq.why: The hot spot comes from key order. Scattering keys spreads writes; splits and extra servers just move the hot end.

hook: Hashing your keys cures timestamp hot spots overnight. What did you just give up?
title: Hash partitioning: even spread, but range scans are gone
body: Timestamp keys pile onto one range. **Hash partitioning** fixes that by computing a hash of the key and using it to pick a shard; the simplest form is `hash(key) mod N` for N shards. A good hash scrambles keys, so consecutive timestamps land on unrelated shards and load spreads evenly. The price: neighbors in key order now live on random shards, so any range query must ask every shard.
takeaway: Hashing buys even load by selling order.
deeper:
**Where it shines:** Point lookups, where each request fetches one key and never asks for a sorted range. Consecutive timestamps hash to unrelated values, so the append hot spot of range partitioning disappears.

**Where it hurts:** A query like 'the last hour of events' must scatter to every shard and gather the results. That multiplies load and exposes each query to the slowest shard, the tail-latency problem at high fan-out.

**What it cannot fix:** A single hot key. A viral video or celebrity profile hashes to exactly one shard whatever function you pick. Even spread is a property of many keys, not of one popular key.

**The catch:** Plain mod N has an operational flaw when N changes: almost every key moves. That is why real systems pair hashing with fixed logical shards or consistent hashing.

quiz.q: After moving an events table from range to hash partitioning, write latency drops but the 'last hour' dashboard gets slow. Why?
quiz.a: Hashing spread the writes evenly, but a time range is now scattered across every shard, so the dashboard query fans out to all of them and waits for the slowest.

mcq.q: A celebrity profile is hammered. Does hash partitioning spread that load?
options: No, one key always hashes to one shard
Yes, the hash scatters its requests evenly
Yes, if the shard count is a prime number
No, unless keys are stored in sorted order
mcq.why: Hashing spreads many keys evenly, but a single key maps to exactly one shard, so its load stays concentrated.

hook: You add an 11th shard to a 10-shard store that uses hash mod N. How much data has to move?
title: hash mod N: add one shard, move 91% of your keys
body: Plain `hash(key) mod N` has a terrible property. Change N and almost every key gets a new remainder, so it moves. Going from 10 to 11 shards, a key stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder mod 10 and mod 11, which holds for about 1 in 11 keys. At petabyte scale, reshuffling nearly everything to add one server saturates the network for a long time.

stat.label: of keys move going from 10 to 11 shards

takeaway: Never let the physical server count appear in your key-to-location formula.
deeper:
**Why caches get a pass:** In a cache, a moved key is just a miss that refetches from the source. That is why hash mod N is rated fit only for simple caches, and even there marked 'avoid'. In a durable store, every moved key is real bytes on the network and disks, competing with user requests.

**Fix 1, fixed logical shards:** Hash into a large, fixed number of logical shards and assign those to servers. Adding a server moves whole logical shards; no key ever changes its logical shard.

**Fix 2, consistent hashing:** Place servers on a hash ring. Adding or removing one moves only about 1/N of keys, the ones next to the change.

**The shared idea:** Both fixes decouple keys from servers. The number in the formula is either frozen forever or irrelevant to most keys.

quiz.q: A durable key-value store uses hash mod N across 10 nodes. Ops wants to add one node on Friday afternoon. What do you warn them about, and what would you change?
quiz.a: About 10/11 of all keys will move, flooding network and disks. Switch to fixed logical shards or consistent hashing so growth moves whole shards or about 1/N of keys.

mcq.q: With hash(key) mod N, roughly what fraction of keys move going from 10 to 11 shards?
options: About 10/11, roughly 91 percent
About 1/11, roughly 9 percent
About half of all keys
Only the keys on one shard
mcq.why: A key stays only if its remainder mod 10 equals its remainder mod 11, which is true for about 1 in 11 keys.

predict.q: A 10-shard store using hash mod N adds an 11th shard. What share of keys move?
options: About 91 percent
About 9 percent
About 50 percent

hook: Uber's Schemaless picked its shard count once and never changed it, while the fleet kept growing. How?
title: Uber fixed 4,096 shards forever and moved shards, not keys
body: Growing a hashed store normally remaps keys. The trick is to create many more **logical shards** than servers and never change that count. Uber's Schemaless (2014-2016) hashed keys into a fixed 4,096 logical shards on top of MySQL, with a separate map assigning logical shards to machines. Adding servers moves whole logical shards; no key ever changes the logical shard it belongs to. Ceph does something similar with placement groups.
takeaway: Hash once into a fixed count. Let only the shard-to-server map change.
deeper:
**Two maps, one frozen:** The key-to-shard function never changes, so there is never a mass reshuffle of individual keys. Only the shard-to-server map changes, in coarse whole-shard units that are easy to copy, verify and switch over.

**Choosing the number is a commitment:** It must be large enough that each server holds several shards, so load can be balanced by moving one at a time. It must also leave room to grow to many more servers without any shard outgrowing a machine. Uber chose 4,096.

**Ceph's version:** Objects hash into a fixed pg_num of placement groups per pool, and CRUSH places groups, not objects, on disks. Unlike a frozen count, Ceph's autoscaler can adjust pg_num as a pool grows.

**Scorecard:** Even spread, no range scans, whole shards move on resize, medium flexibility. Used by Schemaless, Ceph PGs and Vitess.

quiz.q: Your store hashes keys into 16 logical shards on 16 servers. You want to grow to 100 servers. What goes wrong, and what should you have done?
quiz.a: Sixteen shards can occupy at most 16 servers, so the extra servers sit idle unless you remap keys. Start with many more logical shards than servers, like Schemaless's 4,096.

mcq.q: What stays fixed forever in a fixed-logical-shards design like Schemaless?
options: The number of logical shards keys hash into
The number of physical servers
The assignment of shards to servers
The total bytes stored per shard
mcq.why: The logical count never changes, so keys never remap. Only whole logical shards move between servers as the fleet grows.

hook: Add a server and almost every key moves. What layout makes only one existing server notice?
title: Consistent hashing: add a server, move only about 1/N
body: Plain mod N reshuffles almost every key on a membership change. **Consistent hashing** fixes that. Take a ring of hash values from 0 to 2^64. Each server sits where its hashed name lands. Each key hashes onto the same ring and belongs to the next server clockwise. A joining server takes keys only from one neighbor; a leaving server hands its keys to one neighbor. On average only 1/N of the data moves.
takeaway: Change one server, disturb one arc. Everything else stays where it was.
deeper:
**The full lookup:**
1. Hash the key for user 42 to a point on the ring.
2. Walk clockwise to the next virtual node, say vnode A-17 on server A. That is the primary replica.
3. Keep walking and take the next distinct physical servers, B then C, skipping further vnodes on A, so replicas land on different machines.

**Locality of change:** Each server owns only the arc just before its position. Adding a server splits one arc; removing one merges its arc into the next. Compare hash mod N, where changing N remaps almost everything.

**The catch:** Ownership is dictated by hash positions. You cannot freely put a particular shard on a machine because of load, hardware type or region. That limit is why large operators later built directory-style shard managers.

quiz.q: A 10-server consistent-hashing ring loses one server. Which keys move, and roughly what share of the data is that?
quiz.a: Only the failed server's keys, which pass to its clockwise neighbor. That is about 1/N, roughly a tenth of the data; every other key stays put.

mcq.q: On a consistent hashing ring, which server owns a key?
options: The next server clockwise from the key's hash
The server whose hash is numerically closest
The server with the least data at write time
The server chosen by hash(key) mod N
mcq.why: Keys and servers hash onto the same ring; each key belongs to the next server clockwise, so a change affects only one arc.

hook: A few servers share a hash ring. Why might one own 30% of it and another just 5%?
title: Virtual nodes: 100-256 points per server even out the ring
body: With only a few servers, their random points cut the ring into very unequal arcs: one server might own 30 percent and another 5 percent. The fix is **virtual nodes**, or vnodes. Each physical server is placed at many points, for example 100-256. Now each server owns many small arcs scattered around the ring, and the totals come out close to even. Vnodes also let a bigger machine own more arcs than a smaller one.
takeaway: Many small random slices average out. A few big ones never do.
deeper:
**The statistics:** A few random cuts divide a circle badly. The sum of many random pieces per server averages out, so with 100-256 vnodes each, the spread in ownership shrinks enough that no server is badly overloaded.

**Bonus 1, mixed hardware:** Give a machine with twice the capacity twice the vnodes and it takes twice the share of keys.

**Bonus 2, gentler churn:** When a server leaves, its many small arcs are absorbed by many different neighbors instead of dumping everything on one unlucky successor. A joining server takes a little from many servers instead of a lot from one.

**The easy bug:** When picking replicas, walk past vnodes belonging to a physical server you already chose. Skip that step and two copies silently land on the same machine, where one failure takes out both.

quiz.q: Your ring runs 5 servers with one point each, and one server is always overloaded. You add a 6th with one point. Why might that not help, and what would?
quiz.a: One random point may land anywhere, so the imbalance persists. Give every server many vnodes, like 100-256, so each owns many small arcs that average out.

mcq.q: Besides evening out load, what do virtual nodes make easy?
options: Giving a bigger machine a larger share of keys
Running range scans across the ring
Removing the need for replicas
Keeping the ring free of hash collisions
mcq.why: A machine's share is proportional to its vnode count, so a bigger server simply gets more points on the ring.

predict.q: A few servers each sit at one random point on a hash ring. How even is ownership likely to be?
options: Very uneven, like 30% versus 5%
Within about 1% of even
Exactly even, by design

hook: Thousands of people open the same busy Discord channel at once. How does the database see only one query?
title: Discord hashes by channel so one instance can merge requests
body: Amazon's Dynamo paper (SOSP 2007) made consistent hashing with virtual nodes famous, and Cassandra, Riak and many caches adopted it. Discord adds a twist: its Rust data service routes requests by channel ID with consistent hashing, so every request for one channel lands on the same instance. That instance can spot identical concurrent requests and merge them, so the database sees one query instead of thousands. The technique is **request coalescing**.
takeaway: Route duplicates to one place and you can answer them once.
deeper:
**Dynamo's legacy:** It showed a large key-value store could run with no central directory: every node knows the ring, so any node can route any request. The same paper is known for keeping conflicting versions and letting the application merge them.

**Hashing as routing:** Discord uses the ring not only to lay out data but to choose which service instance handles a request. Sending every request for a channel to one instance creates a single place where duplicate in-flight requests are visible.

**Why it matters:** A busy channel is a single hot key. Splitting shards cannot divide one key. Coalescing attacks the duplication itself: one query to the database, one result fanned out to every waiter.

**The catch:** Pure consistent hashing cannot place data by load, fault domain or region on demand, which is why big operators moved to directory-style managers.

quiz.q: Your service instances are picked round-robin, and a viral channel causes thousands of identical database queries. Why can't you coalesce them, and what routing change fixes it?
quiz.a: Identical requests land on different instances, so no one instance sees the duplicates. Route by channel ID with consistent hashing so one instance gets them all and merges them.

mcq.q: Why does Discord route requests by channel ID with consistent hashing?
options: So one instance sees a channel's requests and merges them
So each channel's messages are sorted for range scans
So channels are spread evenly across regions
So a channel's replicas land in separate racks
mcq.why: Routing all of a channel's requests to one instance lets it coalesce identical concurrent requests into a single database query.

hook: A hash function decides where every shard lives. What if you need to move one because of its load or region?
title: Directory partitioning: any shard, anywhere, for any reason
body: Hash-based schemes decide placement for you. In **directory-based partitioning**, a separate service stores an explicit map, such as 'shard 1234 lives on servers X, Y, Z', and clients ask it or cache its answers. You can move any shard anywhere for any reason: load, hardware type, failure domain, region, cost. The price: the directory is now a critical dependency. It must be highly available, and clients must handle stale maps.
takeaway: A directory trades a formula's rigidity for a dependency you must keep alive.
deeper:
**Who uses it:** Google Slicer, Meta Shard Manager, LinkedIn Helix, and the placement layer of most large blob stores. They need to put a shard near its users, keep replicas in separate fault domains, give a hot shard to a quiet machine, and drain a server before upgrading it. No hash function can express those choices.

**The operational bill:** If the directory is down, clients without a cached map cannot find data, so it must be highly available. Cached maps go stale, so a client will sometimes ask a server that no longer owns the shard. The system needs a reject-and-redirect path, and moves must fence writes so two servers never both think they own a shard.

**Scorecard:** Controlled spread. Range scans depend on the design. Data moved on resize: only what you choose. Flexibility: high, the only scheme rated high.

quiz.q: A client's cached directory says shard 7 is on server X, but it moved to Y a minute ago. What must the system do so this is harmless?
quiz.a: Server X must reject the request and redirect the client, which refreshes its map. Moves must also fence writes so X never accepts a write after Y takes ownership.

mcq.q: What is the main cost of directory-based partitioning?
options: A critical map service that clients may see stale
Keys must be sorted before using a directory
Almost every key moves when servers are added
Shards cannot be moved once they are placed
mcq.why: Total placement freedom requires a map service that must stay highly available, and clients must cope with outdated cached copies.

hook: Five sharding schemes, one scorecard. Only one is rated 'high' on flexibility. Which, and what does it cost?
title: Five ways to shard, scored on scans, spread and movement
body: Each scheme wins a different column. **Range**: needs splits to spread, keeps scans, moves only split ranges (Bigtable, Spanner, HBase, CockroachDB). Hash mod N: even, no scans, moves almost everything; simple caches only. Fixed logical shards: even, no scans, moves whole shards (Schemaless, Ceph PGs, Vitess). Consistent hashing with vnodes: even, no scans, moves about 1/N (Dynamo, Cassandra). **Directory**: controlled spread, moves only what you choose, high flexibility (Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix), at the cost of a critical lookup service.
takeaway: Pick the column you can't live without, then read across.
deeper:
**Need scans?** Range partitioning is the only scheme with a clear yes. A directory supports scans only if its shards are ranges.

**Need spread without effort?** Any hash-based scheme delivers it. Range partitioning needs active splitting to stay balanced.

**The column that separates good from bad:** Data moved on resize. Hash mod N moves almost everything and should stay out of durable storage. Fixed logical shards and consistent hashing both keep movement small, one by moving whole shards, the other about 1/N of keys. A directory moves exactly what its controller decides.

**The column that explains the industry:** Flexibility. Google, Meta and LinkedIn needed to place shards by load, fault domain, hardware and region, and to drain servers before upgrades. Only the directory rates high, so all three built central shard managers, often on top of hashing into a large key space.

quiz.q: You need even write spread, cheap growth and no range scans, and you don't want to run a directory service. Which scheme fits?
quiz.a: Hashing into fixed logical shards, or consistent hashing with vnodes. Both spread evenly and move little data on resize without a central map; hash mod N moves too much.

mcq.q: Which scheme moves only whole shards when you resize?
options: Hashing into fixed logical shards
Consistent hashing with vnodes
Plain hash mod N
Range partitioning
mcq.why: Keys map to a fixed set of logical shards forever, so growth just reassigns whole shards to servers. Vnodes move about 1/N of keys.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
hook: Google, Meta and LinkedIn each had a famous ring-based design to copy. Why did all three build something else?
title: Google, Meta and LinkedIn all built central shard managers
body: Every sharded system needs the same hard features: assign shards, move them when servers die, balance load, and never drop requests during a move. Rather than let every team rebuild that, big companies built generic **shard managers**: Google Slicer (2016), Meta Shard Manager (2020-2021), LinkedIn Helix (2012). All three chose a central, directory-style design over pure consistent hashing, because they needed to place by load, fault domain and region, and drain servers before upgrades.
takeaway: When placement needs judgment, a formula can't make it. A directory can.
deeper:
**Why a ring wasn't enough:** Consistent hashing fixes placement by hash position. It cannot say 'keep this shard near its users', 'spread these replicas across fault domains' or 'empty this server before tonight's upgrade'.

**Concentrated expertise:** Handoff protocols, rate-limited moves, fencing during ownership changes and failure detection are subtle. One well-tested implementation serving hundreds of applications beats hundreds of partial ones. Meta's Shard Manager accounts for about 54 percent of sharded applications at Facebook.

**The trade-off:** The shard manager becomes shared critical infrastructure. Its data plane, which routes requests, must be fast and highly available. Its control plane, which decides assignments, can be slower and sit off the request path. Slicer made that split its central idea.

**The lesson:** Every team that shards eventually needs these features. At scale, build them once.

quiz.q: A team proposes pure consistent hashing for a service that must drain hosts before weekly kernel upgrades and keep EU shards in the EU. What's the objection?
quiz.a: A hash ring places by hash position, so it can't pin shards to regions or move them off a host before a restart. That needs a directory-style shard manager.

mcq.q: Why did Slicer, Shard Manager and Helix all pick a directory-style design?
options: They needed placement by load, fault domain and region
Consistent hashing cannot handle more than a few servers
Directories remove the need for any replicas
Hash rings cannot route requests at high throughput
mcq.why: A central map lets them place shards by load, fault domain and region, and move them before planned upgrades, which a ring cannot express.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
hook: Google's sharding service makes careful balancing decisions, yet no request ever waits for them. How?
title: Slicer keeps balancing decisions off the request path
body: A balancer that thinks hard on every request would make every request slow. Google's Slicer (OSDI 2016) splits the job. A **data plane** forwards each request to the right server, fast and reliably. A **control plane** watches load and server health and decides assignments, off the request path. Applications hash keys into a large key space; Slicer divides it into ranges called **slices** and assigns slices to servers.
takeaway: Route fast with today's map. Redraw the map slowly, somewhere else.
deeper:
**Each plane, its own job:** The data plane only needs the current assignment table, but every request passes through it, so it must be quick and highly available. The control plane gathers load statistics and runs balancing logic at its own pace; a slightly late decision slows no individual request.

**Hashing plus a directory:** Hashing into a large key space spreads keys evenly and hides skew in the real keys. Assigning contiguous ranges of that hashed space gives the control plane coarse units to move.

**Three levers:** Give a hot slice more replicas. Split a busy slice. Merge cold slices. All while trying to limit churn, meaning not moving too much at once.

**Why churn matters:** Every move costs network bandwidth and risks a brief disruption. A balancer that chases every small fluctuation spends more moving data than it saves.

quiz.q: Your custom shard router calls a load-balancing optimizer on every request, and p99 spikes whenever the optimizer is slow. What would Slicer's design change?
quiz.a: Separate the planes: the router forwards using a cached assignment, while a control plane recomputes assignments in the background. A slow optimizer then delays rebalancing, not requests.

mcq.q: In Slicer, what does the control plane do?
options: Watches load and health and decides assignments
Forwards every request to the owning server
Stores the application's data on disk
Encrypts traffic between clients and servers
mcq.why: The control plane decides slice assignments off the request path; the data plane just forwards requests using the current assignment.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
hook: Google's auto-sharder served 2-7 million requests per second. Why is that not its most important number?
title: Slicer: the median workload used 63% fewer resources
body: The Slicer paper reports 2-7 million requests per second in production. The number that matters more: the median Slicer-managed workload used 63 percent fewer resources than it would with **static sharding**. Static sharding must provision every shard for its own peak, even though shards peak at different times. A dynamic sharder moves and replicates slices to follow load, so the fleet is sized for combined load, not the sum of peaks.

stat.label: fewer resources for the median Slicer workload

takeaway: Provision every shard for its own peak and you pay for peaks that never coincide.
deeper:
**The static bill:** Each shard gets a fixed server that must survive the shard's worst moment. Across hundreds of shards, most servers idle most of the time, waiting for an occasional peak. Total fleet equals the sum of every shard's peak.

**The dynamic bill:** The control plane splits a slice going hot, adds replicas to share read load, merges cold slices and moves work to quiet servers. The fleet covers actual combined load plus headroom. For the median workload, that gap was 63 percent.

**The same idea elsewhere:** DynamoDB moved from fixed per-partition throughput to table-level admission control because per-partition limits wasted capacity and throttled customers. S3 spreads tenants over huge numbers of drives so bursts cancel out. Tectonic shares spare IOPS across tenants.

**The rule:** Flexibility in where load goes lets you provision for aggregate demand instead of every piece's worst case.

quiz.q: You run 100 static shards, each on its own server sized for that shard's daily peak, and the peaks come at different hours. Where is the waste, and what removes it?
quiz.a: Each server idles outside its own peak, so the fleet equals the sum of peaks. Dynamic sharding moves and replicates slices to follow load, sizing the fleet for combined demand.

mcq.q: Why does static sharding waste capacity?
options: Every shard must be provisioned for its own peak
Static shards cannot be replicated at all
Static shards store data less compactly
Static sharding requires a central directory
mcq.why: Shards peak at different times, but static assignment sizes each for its worst case, so the fleet pays for the sum of peaks.

predict.q: Compared with static sharding, how much less did the median Slicer-managed workload use in resources?
options: 63 percent less
6 percent less
About the same

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
hook: A solver could find the perfect layout for a million machines. Why do real systems settle for 'good enough'?
title: Meta Shard Manager: 1M+ machines, no time for perfect
body: Meta's Shard Manager does Slicer's job at Meta. A 2020 blog post said it managed tens of millions of shards on hundreds of thousands of servers across hundreds of applications. The SOSP 2021 paper says it runs on over one million machines and handles about 54 percent of Facebook's sharded applications. Applications declare **placement constraints**, such as spreading replicas across fault domains or keeping a shard near its users, and a constrained optimizer balances CPU, memory and storage.
takeaway: A perfect placement that arrives late loses to a good one that arrives now.
deeper:
**Placement as optimization:** Each application states what it needs, and the system searches for an assignment that respects fault-domain spread, locality to users and resource limits across several dimensions at once. Balancing only shard count would leave some machines out of memory while others run out of CPU.

**The honest limit:** The paper notes that a full constraint solver is too slow for near-real-time placement at global scale. When a server fails or load shifts, the system has to respond quickly, so practical systems use faster heuristics that find good-enough assignments in time.

**Geography is the default:** The paper's first observation is that most applications need geo-distribution. A shard manager that places only within one cluster is not enough; it must place shards across regions. That ties shard management to leader placement and data residency.

quiz.q: Your placement service runs an exact solver that takes 40 minutes per run. A rack fails. What's wrong with this design at scale, and what do practical systems do?
quiz.a: Placement must react in near real time, and a full solver is too slow at global scale. Practical shard managers use fast heuristics that give good-enough assignments quickly.

mcq.q: Why do practical shard managers fall back on heuristics?
options: A full constraint solver is too slow at global scale
Heuristics give provably optimal placements
Constraint solvers cannot model fault domains
Heuristics remove the need for a directory
mcq.why: Meta's paper notes a full solver is too slow for near-real-time placement at global scale, so faster heuristics are used.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
hook: Shard managers are famous for surviving crashes. Meta found something else matters far more. What?
title: Planned restarts happen about 1,000× more often than crashes
body: Meta's Shard Manager paper found that **planned events**, such as software upgrades, happen about 1,000 times more often than unplanned failures. So the most important feature is not crash recovery. It is moving shards and handing off primaries gracefully before a planned restart. A system that only handles failures well makes every routine deploy look like a crash to clients: timeouts, retries, and a steady drip of small outages.

stat.label: more planned events than unplanned failures

takeaway: Design for the restart you schedule, not just the crash you fear.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** A large fleet deploys new software often, and each deploy restarts many servers. Hardware crashes are comparatively rare. If every restart drops that server's shards until clients time out and failover kicks in, planned events dominate unavailability.

**Drain, then restart:**
1. The shard manager learns a server will restart.
2. It moves that server's shards elsewhere or promotes a replica on another server to primary.
3. Only then does the restart proceed, and clients see a clean handoff instead of errors.

**Same idea at LinkedIn:** Venice, built on Helix, lists rolling restarts as a feature for exactly this reason.

**Ask this in a review:** Not only 'how does it recover from a crash?' but 'how does it drain and hand off before a planned event?' The second path runs about 1,000 times as often.

quiz.q: Your failover is excellent: a crashed primary is replaced in 30 seconds. Yet users see errors every day during deploys. What's the design gap?
quiz.a: Deploys are handled like crashes. Planned events are about 1,000 times more common, so the system should hand off primaries and move shards before each restart instead of waiting for failover.

mcq.q: What did Meta conclude from planned events outnumbering failures about 1,000 to 1?
options: Graceful handoff before restarts matters most
Crash recovery should be made much faster
Upgrades should be scheduled less often
Shards should never have a primary replica
mcq.why: Since planned restarts dominate, moving shards and handing off primaries before a restart matters more for availability than crash recovery alone.

predict.q: At Meta's scale, how do planned events like upgrades compare in frequency with unplanned failures?
options: About 1,000 times more frequent
About equally frequent
About 10 times less frequent

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
hook: LinkedIn's apps don't write failover code. They list a few states and legal moves. Who does the rest?
title: Helix runs every replica as a state machine
body: Hand-written failover code is where clusters break. LinkedIn's Apache Helix, described at SoCC 2012 as a generic cluster management framework, models each replica with a **state machine**, for example OFFLINE, SLAVE, MASTER. The application declares its states and allowed transitions. When nodes join, fail or restart, Helix computes the transitions needed and orchestrates them across the cluster. LinkedIn's derived-data store Venice uses it for placement, rack awareness, rebalancing and rolling restarts.
takeaway: Declare the states and legal moves. Let one engine drive the cluster there.
deeper:
**A precise vocabulary:** Every replica is in a known state, and every change is an explicit transition: promote a replica to MASTER after the old one fails, take one OFFLINE before a restart. Helix computes a target state for the whole cluster and issues the transitions to reach it.

**What Venice gets:**
1. Partition-replica placement: which nodes hold which replicas.
2. Rack-aware placement: a partition's copies are not all in one rack.
3. Automatic rebalancing when nodes fail.
4. Rolling restarts, node by node, without losing availability.

**Where it fits:** Helix is the oldest of the three shard managers, dating to 2012. With Slicer and Shard Manager, it marks the industry's convergence on central, directory-style cluster management.

**The payoff:** Failover stops being custom code in every service and becomes declared rules that one well-tested engine enforces.

quiz.q: A partition's MASTER node dies. In Helix terms, what happens next, and who decides it?
quiz.a: Helix sees the failure, computes a new target state, and issues transitions, such as promoting a SLAVE replica elsewhere to MASTER. The app only defined the states and allowed transitions.

mcq.q: How does Helix model each replica?
options: As a state machine with states like OFFLINE and MASTER
As a point on a consistent hashing ring
As an entry in a CRUSH cluster map
As a token bucket with a refill rate
mcq.why: Helix gives each replica a state machine and computes the transitions needed when nodes join, fail or restart.

hook: A shard is too big and needs to split right now. How do you split it without moving a single byte?
title: Split a shard in place now, move a child later
body: Data does not grow evenly: some shards get big, some hot, some nearly empty, and the system must reshape them while serving traffic. **Splitting** turns one shard into two; for range partitioning, pick a split key and create two child ranges. The new child can start on the same server, so no data moves at first, and be moved later. **Merging** is the reverse: combining small adjacent shards to cut per-shard overhead.
takeaway: Make the split a metadata change. Make the move a separate, slower job.
deeper:
**Why split in place:** A split becomes a cheap metadata update: new boundaries are recorded and both children keep serving from the same machine. Moving one child is a separate, rate-limited rebalancing step that can happen when convenient. That keeps splits fast, which matters when a shard is getting hot and needs relief.

**Why merge at all:** After heavy deletes, you can be left with many tiny shards. Each carries fixed overhead regardless of size: memory, open file handles, and in consensus systems a Raft group with its own leader and heartbeats. Thousands of near-empty shards waste real resources. Spanner and CockroachDB merge small adjacent ranges.

**The hash-world equivalent:** With fixed logical shards the boundaries never change, so the only reshaping move is reassigning whole shards among servers.

quiz.q: After a big data purge, your cluster has 50,000 ranges, most nearly empty, and memory use is still high. Why, and what fixes it?
quiz.a: Each range carries fixed overhead (memory, file handles, a Raft group) regardless of size. Merging small adjacent ranges cuts the count and that overhead.

mcq.q: Why can a range split start with no data movement?
options: The new child can stay on the same server at first
Splits only change the hash function
The old shard is deleted before the split
Replicas already hold both halves elsewhere
mcq.why: A split records a new boundary; both children keep serving from the same server, and one is moved later by rebalancing.

hook: You must move a live shard to a new server while writes keep arriving. How long do writes have to stop?
title: Moving a live shard: copy, catch up, fence, switch
body: **Rebalancing** moves shards so each server carries a fair load, usually in four steps. Copy a snapshot of the shard to the new server. Stream new writes, the log, until the new copy catches up. Briefly pause or fence writes, switch ownership in the directory, and resume. Delete the old copy after a safety delay. The shard stays available throughout, with only a brief write pause at the switch.
takeaway: Copy the bulk while live. Stop the world only for the handoff.
deeper:
**Snapshot:** Copies the bulk of the data while the old server keeps serving. Writes continue, so the snapshot is stale the moment it finishes.

**Log stream:** Replays new writes on the destination until it is nearly current, shrinking the gap to almost nothing.

**The fence:** The critical moment. Writes are paused or rejected very briefly so no write lands on the old owner after the new owner takes over. Ownership flips in the directory, clients are redirected, writes resume. Clients with stale cached maps must get a redirect, not an error.

**Safety delay:** If the new copy is incomplete or the new server dies right away, the old copy is still there. Deleting it immediately would turn a routine move into potential data loss. The same pattern underlies graceful handoff before planned restarts.

quiz.q: During a shard move, ownership switches without fencing, and a client with a stale map writes to the old server a second later. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: The write lands on a server that no longer owns the shard, so it is lost or the copies diverge. Fencing blocks writes during the switch so only one owner ever accepts them.

mcq.q: Why keep the old copy for a while after a shard move?
options: In case the new copy is incomplete or its server fails
To serve reads faster from two servers at once
Because the directory updates only once a day
To let the log stream finish replaying
mcq.why: The safety delay keeps a fallback; deleting immediately would turn a failed or incomplete move into data loss.

hook: A new empty rack arrives and the balancer gets straight to work. Why does user latency spike for hours?
title: Rebalancing isn't free: a new rack can flood the network
body: Moving a shard copies real bytes over real networks and disks. A naive balancer sees a new, empty rack, spots a huge imbalance, and fills it immediately with many parallel copies. That can **saturate the network** for hours, starving user requests of bandwidth and pushing latency up across the cluster. The fix: cap the move rate and watch user latency while moves run, so balancing happens quietly in the background.
takeaway: The fastest rebalance is often a self-inflicted outage. Slow and invisible wins.
deeper:
**Shared resources:** Rebalancing competes with user traffic for the same network links, disk heads and storage-node CPU. On hard drives with limited IOPS, and across shared top-of-rack and cluster links, a burst of parallel copies can dominate the hardware.

**The same discipline, repeated:** Slicer tries to limit churn. Continuous add-and-retire requires new capacity to be filled gradually through rate-limited rebalancing. Background work such as compaction, scrubbing and rebalancing is a named source of tail latency, which is why Tectonic runs background work in a lower TrafficClass.

**What good looks like:**
1. A global move-rate limit.
2. Per-node limits on concurrent moves.
3. A feedback signal from user-facing latency: if it climbs, the balancer slows down.

**The goal:** Not the fastest convergence, but reaching balance without users noticing.

quiz.q: After adding 10 racks, your cluster's p99 read latency triples for six hours, then recovers on its own. What likely happened, and what would you change?
quiz.a: The balancer rushed to fill the new racks, saturating network and disks with copies. Cap the move rate, limit concurrent moves per node, and slow down when user latency rises.

mcq.q: What is the recommended guard against rebalancing hurting users?
options: Cap the move rate and watch user latency
Rebalance only when a disk fails
Fill new racks as fast as possible
Disable replicas during rebalancing
mcq.why: Moves use the same network and disks as users; rate limits and a latency feedback loop keep balancing in the background.

predict.q: A balancer fills a brand-new empty rack as fast as it can. The most likely result:
options: Saturated network and high user latency for hours
Balanced in minutes with no user impact
The new rack's disks wear out early

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: Three copies of your data on three separate disks, and one failure still destroys all three. How?
title: Three copies in one server protect almost nothing
body: Placement decides which disks hold a shard's copies, and its main goal is that one failure never destroys them all. A **failure domain** is a set of components that fail together: a disk, a server, a rack sharing a top-of-rack switch and power, a row, a power zone, a building, an availability zone, a region. Three copies on three disks in one server give almost no protection. Three racks survive a rack failure. Three zones survive a zone outage.
takeaway: Count copies by failure domain, not by disk.
deeper:
**Small and frequent to big and rare:** Disks fail most often. A server can die from a bad power supply or motherboard and take every disk inside with it. A rack shares a switch and power feed, so one fault drops every server in it. Rows, power zones, buildings, zones and regions fail less often but take more with them.

**The rule for copies:** Replicas and erasure-coded fragments both follow it. Your protection is set by the smallest failure domain that contains all copies. Three copies in three zones of one region survive a zone outage but not a regional disaster, which is why some data is also replicated across regions.

**Encoded in real systems:** Ceph's CRUSH uses a cluster-map tree like root, datacenter, rack, host, disk, with rules such as 'pick 3 different racks'. LinkedIn's Venice uses Helix for rack-aware placement. Meta's Shard Manager lets applications spread replicas across fault domains.

quiz.q: Your three replicas sit in three racks, all fed by the same power zone. What do you survive, and which failure takes out everything?
quiz.a: You survive disk, server and single-rack failures. A power-zone failure hits all three racks at once, because they share that failure domain.

mcq.q: Why is a rack treated as a failure domain?
options: Its servers share a top-of-rack switch and power
Its disks all come from one manufacturer
It holds exactly one replica of each shard
It is the unit that erasure coding encodes
mcq.why: Servers in a rack share a top-of-rack switch and power, so one fault can take all of them down together.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: An RS(10,4) stripe survives losing any 4 of 14 fragments. How few racks can it use and survive a rack loss?
title: RS(10,4) needs at least 4 racks to survive a rack loss
body: A Reed-Solomon **RS(10,4)** stripe has 10 data and 4 parity fragments, 14 in total, and survives the loss of any 4. To survive a full rack failure, no rack may hold more than 4 of the 14 fragments, so you need at least 4 racks, laid out 4+4+4+2. Surviving a whole zone loss would need at least 4 zones. That is why many systems use erasure coding inside a datacenter and full replication across regions.
takeaway: Fragments per domain must never exceed the losses the code can absorb.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** Losing 4 fragments is fine; losing 5 is data loss. If one rack held 5, a single rack failure would destroy the stripe. Capping each rack at 4 means 14 fragments need ceil(14/4) = 4 racks.

**Why zones hurt:** Spreading every stripe over at least 4 zones means a read that needs 10 fragments pulls most of them across zone links, and every repair moves data between zones. Racks in one datacenter share fast, cheap networking, so erasure coding works well there. Across regions the network is slower and costlier, and a regional read wants its data locally.

**The common result:** A two-level design. Erasure coding within a datacenter for cheap durability against disk, server and rack failures. Full replicas in other regions for regional disasters and local reads.

**Bonus use:** The same redundancy doubles as a tail-latency tool: request extra fragments and ignore slow disks.

quiz.q: A teammate spreads an RS(10,4) stripe over 3 racks as 5+5+4. What happens when one rack fails, and what layout fixes it?
quiz.a: Losing a 5-fragment rack loses 5 of 14, one more than RS(10,4) tolerates, so the stripe is gone. Use at least 4 racks with at most 4 fragments each, like 4+4+4+2.

mcq.q: Why do many systems erasure-code within a datacenter but replicate across regions?
options: Zone-proof stripes need 4+ zones and cross-zone reads
Erasure coding cannot survive a rack failure
Replication uses less storage than erasure coding
Regions forbid erasure-coded data by law
mcq.why: Surviving a zone loss with RS(10,4) needs at least 4 zones, so reads and repairs cross slow links; racks share cheap datacenter networking.

predict.q: An RS(10,4) stripe (14 fragments, survives any 4 lost) must survive a full rack failure. Minimum racks?
options: 4 racks
2 racks
14 racks

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: Ceph clients find any object's disks without asking a lookup service. How do they all agree?
title: CRUSH computes where data lives instead of looking it up
body: A central directory is one more service on every read path. Ceph's **CRUSH** (Controlled Replication Under Scalable Hashing, 2006) computes locations instead. Its paper calls it a scalable pseudo-random data distribution function that maps objects to storage devices without a central directory, following user-defined policies that separate replicas across failure domains. Every client holds the same **cluster map**, so every client computes the same answer, with no central lookup on the read path.
takeaway: If everyone holds the same map and function, nobody needs to ask.
deeper:
**Between hashing and a directory:** Like hashing, CRUSH is deterministic, so any client can find data without asking a server. That removes a directory as a bottleneck on reads. Unlike a plain hash, its inputs include a description of the physical cluster and a policy, so the output respects failure domains.

**The weighted tree:** The cluster map is a tree like root, datacenter, rack, host, disk, with weights. Weights let bigger disks receive proportionally more data, which lets fleets mix disk sizes as racks are continuously added and retired.

**Gentle growth:** When a disk is added, CRUSH moves only a proportional share of placement groups to it, similar in spirit to consistent hashing.

**The catch:** Placement comes from the function and the map, not a free per-group choice made for load reasons. Directory-based placement is more flexible and can be heat-aware.

quiz.q: A Ceph client and a storage node both need to know where placement group 7.3a lives. Neither calls a lookup service. Why do they get the same answer?
quiz.a: Both run the deterministic CRUSH function on the same PG ID, the same cluster map and the same rule, so they compute identical lists of OSDs.

mcq.q: What lets every Ceph client compute the same data location?
options: All clients share the cluster map and run CRUSH
A central directory caches every location
Each object stores its own location list
Clients broadcast a query to all OSDs
mcq.why: CRUSH is deterministic; with the same cluster map and rules, every client computes the same OSDs without a lookup.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: Ceph finds the three disks for any object in two hops, with no lookup. What's the stop in the middle?
title: Ceph's two hops: object to placement group to disks
body: Ceph places data in two steps. First, hash the object name and map it to one of `pg_num` **placement groups** (PGs) in the pool; a PG is a bucket of many objects. Second, CRUSH takes the PG ID, the cluster map (a weighted tree like root, datacenter, rack, host, disk) and a rule such as 'pick 3 different racks, then 1 disk in each'. It outputs the list of OSDs, meaning disks, for that PG.
takeaway: Map objects to a fixed set of groups, then place groups, not objects.
deeper:
**One object, end to end:**
1. The name is hashed; hash(name) mod pg_num selects placement group 7.3a.
2. CRUSH gets the PG ID, the cluster map of root, racks, hosts, disks and weights, and a rule of 3 replicas in different racks.
3. Out come OSD 12 in rack 1, OSD 88 in rack 4 and OSD 203 in rack 7: three copies in three failure domains.

**A familiar pattern:** Step one is the fixed-logical-shards idea. pg_num is the logical count, and objects map to PGs by a simple function. Growth is handled in step two, where CRUSH remaps whole PGs onto a changing set of disks.

**Rules set protection:** Change the rule to 'pick 3 different datacenters' and the protection level changes without touching how objects map to PGs.

quiz.q: You add 20 disks to a Ceph pool without changing pg_num. Which of the two mapping steps changes for existing objects?
quiz.a: Only step two. Objects still hash to the same PGs; CRUSH, with the updated cluster map, moves some whole PGs to the new disks.

mcq.q: In Ceph, what does CRUSH take as input to choose OSDs?
options: The PG ID, the cluster map and a placement rule
The object's full name and its size
The client's IP address and region
The last OSD that stored the object
mcq.why: Step two feeds CRUSH the placement group ID, the weighted cluster map and a rule like 3 replicas in different racks.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: Why would Ceph deliberately track data in coarse buckets instead of object by object?
title: Ceph tracks thousands of PGs, not millions of objects
body: Tracking millions of objects one by one, each with its own location and replication state, is too costly. **Placement groups** bundle many objects, so Ceph tracks and peers thousands of groups instead. The count needs balance. Ceph's docs say `mon_target_pg_per_osd` defaults to 100 and recommend about 200, warning that values above 500 can cause excessive **peering** traffic and memory use. An autoscaler can change `pg_num` as the pool grows.
takeaway: Any per-item cost at scale must be paid per group, not per item.
deeper:
**What peering is:** The OSDs holding a PG agree on its current state, for example after a disk restarts. It happens per PG, so the PG count directly sets coordination overhead.

**Too few or too many:** With too few PGs, each is a coarse chunk, so data spreads unevenly and recovery after a failure involves few disks working in parallel. With too many, every OSD spends memory and network on bookkeeping and peering chatter, which is why Ceph warns against going above 500 per OSD.

**Why an autoscaler:** The right pg_num depends on how many OSDs a pool spans and how much data it holds, and both change. Ceph adjusts pg_num as the pool grows instead of making operators guess once and live with it.

**The general lesson:** Count objects, not only bytes, and amortize per-item costs by grouping items into units the control plane can manage.

quiz.q: An operator sets 1,000 PGs per OSD to get finer-grained balance. What does Ceph warn will happen?
quiz.a: Above about 500 PGs per OSD, peering traffic and memory use become excessive, because each PG needs its own state tracking and peering.

mcq.q: What does Ceph recommend as a PG-per-OSD target?
options: About 200, with 100 as the default
About 10, to minimize peering
About 1,000, for finer balance
Exactly one PG per stored object
mcq.why: Ceph's docs: mon_target_pg_per_osd defaults to 100, about 200 is recommended, and above 500 risks excessive peering traffic and memory.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: One S3 customer's workload might touch over a million disks. Why scatter one customer that widely?
title: S3 may spread one workload over a million disks, on purpose
body: Placing copies safely is only half of placement. The other half is **heat**: in Andy Warfield's 2023 description of S3, the number of requests hitting a given disk at any point in time. Put many hot objects on one drive and its few IOPS become a hot spot. So S3 intentionally puts different objects onto different sets of drives, spreading each customer's accesses over a very large number of disks. A single customer workload might be served by over a million disks.
takeaway: Scatter every customer thin enough and no single disk can be their bottleneck.
deeper:
**Why big drives need it:** Large hard drives have few random IOPS relative to their capacity. If an unlucky placement puts several hot objects on one drive, its small IOPS budget runs out and requests queue, even while the fleet as a whole has plenty of spare capacity.

**Placement as load spreading:** Instead of keeping a customer's objects together, S3 deliberately scatters them across different drive sets. Each customer touches a vast number of disks, and each disk carries a thin slice of many customers' traffic. When one customer gets busy, the extra load divides among so many drives that none is pushed over the edge.

**Why a directory helps:** Directory-style placement can decide freely where each object goes, so it can be heat-aware. A fixed function like CRUSH optimizes for failure-domain separation and even capacity instead.

quiz.q: Design A keeps each customer's objects on a dedicated set of 50 drives; design B scatters every customer across the whole fleet. One customer's traffic spikes 20×. Which copes, and why?
quiz.a: B. The spike spreads over a huge number of drives, each getting a sliver, while in A the same 50 drives' limited IOPS are overwhelmed.

mcq.q: What does 'heat' mean in S3's placement design?
options: Requests hitting a disk at a point in time
The physical temperature of a busy drive
The fraction of a disk's capacity in use
How recently an object was last written
mcq.why: Warfield defines heat as the number of requests hitting a given disk at any point in time; clustered hot objects make a drive a hot spot.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: Every S3 customer is bursty. So why is the load on each individual S3 disk smooth?
title: At huge scale, independent bursts cancel out
body: Individual workloads are very bursty. Warfield's key insight about S3 is aggregation: once you combine enough of them, it becomes difficult or impossible for any single workload to move the aggregate peak. While one customer spikes, others are quiet. Because each drive serves a thin slice of very many customers, drive-level demand stays smooth. Small clusters do not get this, because they serve too few workloads for **bursts to average away**.
takeaway: One tenant is unpredictable. A million tenants are a forecast.
deeper:
**The insurance mapping:** One household's claims are unpredictable, but the claims of millions of households are stable. Swap households for tenants and claims for request bursts and the mapping holds: a single tenant can spike sharply without warning, yet the sum across a huge population of independent tenants barely moves.

**Two ingredients:** Enormous scale, with one customer workload possibly touching over a million disks. And deliberate spreading, so every disk mixes traffic from many unrelated customers. Spreading makes each disk see the aggregate, not any individual workload, which is why big, slow, cheap drives can keep up.

**Same principle elsewhere:** It explains Slicer's savings over static sharding, and why multi-tenancy saves money: one team's idle capacity serves another team's peak.

**The catch:** It depends on scale. A cluster with a handful of large tenants sees their bursts add up, not cancel, so it must reserve explicit headroom.

quiz.q: Your internal object store has 4 huge tenants on 200 drives, and you copy S3 by using dense, cheap hard drives with no spare IOPS. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: With only 4 tenants, bursts don't cancel; two spiking together overload the drives. Aggregation only smooths load across very many independent workloads, so you need explicit headroom.

mcq.q: Why can S3 use slow, cheap drives despite bursty customers?
options: Each disk sees the smooth sum of many workloads
Customers are rate-limited to a flat request rate
S3 moves bursty customers onto flash
Disks sit idle between customer bursts
mcq.why: Spread thinly over huge numbers of drives, independent bursts cancel out, so no single workload moves any drive's peak much.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
hook: S3 serves hot data from big, slow, cheap hard drives. Why would the same choice sink a smaller cluster?
title: Cheap slow drives only work at hyperscale
body: Heat-aware placement is why a hyperscale object store can use big, slow, cheap hard drives. Each drive has few IOPS, but spreading every tenant thinly across millions of drives means no single drive gets too many hot requests. A smaller system does not get this for free. Without that many drives and tenants, bursts add up instead of cancelling. You must **reserve IOPS headroom** or put hot data on flash.
takeaway: Don't copy a hyperscaler's hardware without copying its scale.
deeper:
**The trap in a design review:** Someone notes that S3 runs on dense hard drives and concludes a smaller internal store can too. The economics behind S3, very low IOPS per terabyte offset by statistical smoothing across a huge fleet, do not transfer to a few hundred drives and a few dozen tenants.

**What goes wrong small:** One tenant's burst lands on a noticeable fraction of the drives. A few simultaneous bursts overload them.

**Two remedies, two bills:** Reserving IOPS headroom means buying more drives than capacity alone requires, paying for spindles you keep partly idle. Using flash for hot data means paying more per terabyte for far more IOPS, plus tiering logic to decide what is hot.

**The honest question:** Which of these are you paying for, and does your capacity model count IOPS as well as bytes? Bytes and operations scale separately.

quiz.q: Your 200-drive object store keeps missing latency SLOs during batch jobs, though it's only 50 percent full. What are your two options?
quiz.a: Reserve IOPS headroom by adding drives beyond what capacity needs, or move hot data to flash. At this scale bursts don't cancel, so free bytes aren't free IOPS.

mcq.q: What must a small storage system do instead of relying on heat spreading?
options: Reserve IOPS headroom or use flash for hot data
Use larger hard drives to gain more IOPS
Pack each tenant onto dedicated drives
Run drives closer to their IOPS limits
mcq.why: Without hyperscale aggregation, bursts add up, so you need spare IOPS or faster media for hot data.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: A celebrity, a viral video, a timestamp key, a batch job. Why can't one fix handle every hot spot?
title: Five causes of hot spots, and why each needs its own fix
body: A **hot spot**, or hot partition, is a shard that gets much more traffic than others. Causes include a celebrity profile, a viral video, a sequential key like timestamps, a big customer, or a batch job scanning one range. It matters because one overloaded server can throttle requests while the rest of the cluster sits idle. And the causes come in different shapes: a hot range, a single hot key, a sequential pattern, a noisy tenant.
takeaway: Name the shape of the heat before you pick the cure.
deeper:
**Ranges split, keys don't:** When many different keys in one range are busy, splitting the range divides load between two servers. A single hot key, like one celebrity profile or one viral video, cannot be split; it needs caching, read replicas, request coalescing or key salting.

**Sequential keys move the heat:** Timestamps just shift the hot spot to the newest range after each split. They need a different key design.

**Tenants are a different problem:** A big customer or a batch job is really a multi-tenancy issue, handled by admission control, quotas and priority classes, as in DynamoDB's table-level token buckets and Tectonic's traffic classes.

**Detecting it:** Monitor consumed throughput per shard, and ideally a histogram of which keys inside it are busy. DynamoDB uses exactly that signal to decide whether a split will help and where to cut.

quiz.q: One shard runs at 10× average load, and 95 percent of its requests are for one key. Will splitting help? What would you try?
quiz.a: No: one key can't be divided, so it stays whole in one child. Cache it, add read replicas, coalesce duplicate requests, or salt it if the load is writes.

mcq.q: Which hot-spot cause is best treated as a multi-tenancy problem?
options: A big customer whose traffic dwarfs others
A timestamp key where writes hit one end
A single viral video everyone requests
A range of many busy neighboring keys
mcq.why: A big customer or batch job is handled with admission control, quotas and priority classes, not by splitting or key design.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: A DynamoDB table outgrew a partition, so it was split in two. Why did its hottest keys get slower?
title: Early DynamoDB: splitting for size also split throughput
body: Early DynamoDB divided a table's provisioned throughput evenly across partitions. The paper's example: if a partition can hold at most 1,000 write capacity units (WCUs) and a table has 3,200, you get four partitions of 800 WCUs each. That assumed uniform access, which real workloads rarely have. Worse was **throughput dilution**: splitting a partition for size also split its throughput, so the hot half got less capacity than before. Customers were throttled though their table total was high enough.
takeaway: Enforce limits per partition and skew becomes throttling you already paid for.
deeper:
**Why the paper matters:** DynamoDB's 2022 USENIX ATC paper is one of the best public accounts of hot-spot handling, because it shows the design evolving step by step, each step fixing the last one's failure.

**Dilution in action:** A partition grows too large and is split for size. If most traffic hits one half, that half now has only part of the old capacity, though nothing about the workload or the table's total changed. More data made the hot keys slower.

**The root cause:** Limits enforced at the partition level. In the paper's words, application workloads frequently have non-uniform access patterns both over time and over key ranges. Even division means a partition carrying more than its share gets throttled while cold partitions' capacity goes unused.

**The pattern:** It is the same kind of waste static sharding causes: capacity pinned to pieces instead of shared by the whole.

quiz.q: A table has 3,200 WCUs across four 800-WCU partitions, and 90 percent of writes hit one partition. What happens, and why doesn't the table total help?
quiz.a: That partition needs about 2,880 WCUs but is capped at 800, so writes throttle. Limits are per partition, so the other partitions' unused capacity can't be borrowed.

mcq.q: What was throughput dilution in early DynamoDB?
options: Splitting a partition for size also split its throughput
Replication diluting writes across three zones
Throughput dropping steadily as tables aged
Burst credits expiring after 300 seconds
mcq.why: A size split divided the partition's throughput too, so a hot half ended up with less capacity than before the split.

predict.q: Early DynamoDB splits a hot partition in two because it grew too large. What happens to the hot keys' throughput?
options: It drops, because throughput was split too
It doubles, because there are two partitions
It stays exactly the same

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: DynamoDB added burst credits and automatic boosts for hot partitions. Why did customers still get throttled?
title: Bursting and adaptive capacity patched per-partition limits
body: DynamoDB's first fixes were **bursting** and **adaptive capacity**.
