Bursting let a partition spend unused capacity saved from up to the last 300 seconds, if its storage node also had spare capacity, which absorbed short spikes. Adaptive capacity watched for long-lived skew and boosted partitions that stayed hot. Both helped. But both were reactive and still tied to per-partition limits, so the enforcement unit, the partition, never changed.
takeaway: Patching a limit reactively still leaves the wrong thing being limited.
deeper:
**Bursting as savings:** A quiet partition banks unused throughput for up to 300 seconds and can spend it during a short spike. The condition that the storage node also have spare capacity matters: bursting borrows from the physical machine, so it cannot promise capacity the node does not have.

**Adaptive capacity:** Targeted the other pattern, a partition that stays hot for a long time. It detected sustained skew and raised the hot partition's limit, reducing throttling for stable hot spots.

**Why it wasn't enough:** Reactive means a hot partition must first be noticed, then boosted. And because enforcement was still per partition, the design flaw from step 1 remained.

**What came next:** Step 3 changed the enforcement unit itself, moving limits from partitions to tables. Bursting also packed nodes beyond their provisioned totals, which later required balancing consumed capacity across storage nodes.

quiz.q: A partition idles for 10 minutes, then gets a 30-second spike well above its limit. Its storage node is busy with other tenants. Does bursting absorb the spike?
quiz.a: Not necessarily. Bursting spends saved capacity (up to 300 seconds' worth) only if the storage node also has spare capacity; a busy node can't lend it.

mcq.q: What limited both bursting and adaptive capacity?
options: They were reactive and tied to per-partition limits
They required customers to resize tables manually
They worked only for read traffic
They moved data between regions to relieve load
mcq.why: Both responded to skew rather than changing the enforcement unit, which remained the individual partition.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: A hot partition hits its limit while the rest of the table idles. What had to change so it could borrow?
title: DynamoDB moved the limit from the partition to the table
body: Per-partition limits throttled hot partitions while cold ones wasted capacity. DynamoDB replaced adaptive capacity with **global admission control** (GAC), a service that tracks token buckets at the table level. Request routers keep local token buckets and refill them from GAC every few seconds. Now the limit applies to the table as a whole, so a hot partition can use capacity the cold partitions leave unused. Partition-level buckets stay as defense in depth.
takeaway: Limit what the customer bought, the table, not how you happened to slice it.
deeper:
**Token buckets:** Tokens refill at a fixed rate, each request takes one, and an empty bucket means reject or delay. GAC applies this at the level the customer pays for. Traffic can shift freely among partitions as long as the table total stays in budget, which cures throughput dilution.

**Fast by design:** Checking a central service on every request would add latency and a bottleneck. Routers admit requests from their local buckets and only refill from GAC every few seconds.

**Why partition buckets remain:** Storage nodes host thousands of replicas from unrelated customers. DynamoDB caps partition-level buckets so one application cannot consume all or a significant share of a node's resources. GAC gives a customer flexibility across partitions; the caps protect everyone else on the hardware.

**The catch:** GAC cannot help when one partition needs more than one storage node can deliver.

quiz.q: With GAC, a table's hot partition wants 3× its old share, and total table traffic is still under budget. What limits it now?
quiz.a: The table-level budget lets it borrow cold partitions' unused capacity, but the partition-level cap and what one storage node can deliver still bound it.

mcq.q: Where does GAC enforce DynamoDB's throughput limit?
options: At the table level, via router token buckets
Per partition, split evenly across partitions
Per storage node, based on disk usage
Per client connection, by IP address
mcq.why: Routers hold local token buckets refilled from GAC, enforcing the table's total so hot partitions can use unused table capacity.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: A partition is small but swamped with traffic. Where should you cut it in two?
title: Split for consumption: cut where the traffic divides
body: Even with table-level limits, one partition can need more than one storage node can deliver. So DynamoDB splits by consumed throughput: once a partition crosses a threshold, it is **split for consumption**, with the split point chosen from the key distribution it has observed. Load divides, not just data. Splits usually complete in minutes. DynamoDB also detects a single hot item or a sequential key range and skips those useless splits.
takeaway: Split where the requests divide, not where the bytes do.
deeper:
**The flowchart:**
1. Monitor each partition's consumed throughput and a key histogram.
2. Below the split threshold? Keep watching.
3. Above it, check whether traffic is on a single key or a sequential range. If so, don't split; rely on admission control and caching.
4. Otherwise choose a split point from the observed key distribution, create two child partitions, and move a child to a less loaded node if needed.

**Size split versus consumption split:** A size split picks the middle of the data. A consumption split picks the point that divides the requests evenly, which can be far from the data midpoint.

**Principled exclusions:** One key cannot be divided, so a single hot item stays whole in one child. A sequential pattern just moves the hot end into whichever child holds the top of the range.

quiz.q: A partition holds keys A-Z, but 80 percent of requests hit keys A-C. Where would a consumption split cut, compared with a size split?
quiz.a: Near the point that divides requests evenly, inside the A-C range, rather than at the data midpoint around M. A size split would leave nearly all the load in one child.

mcq.q: When does DynamoDB deliberately skip a split-for-consumption?
options: When traffic is on one item or a sequential range
When the partition is below its size limit
When the table uses global admission control
When the partition has only three replicas
mcq.why: One key can't be divided and a sequential pattern just moves the hot end, so DynamoDB detects these and avoids useless splits.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: Letting partitions burst made customers happy. Why did it leave some DynamoDB storage nodes overbooked?
title: DynamoDB overbooked its nodes, then balanced by real use
body: Once partitions could burst and share table-level capacity, storage nodes ended up packed beyond their provisioned totals: their replicas together might use more than the node can deliver. Rather than return to rigid caps, DynamoDB balances **consumed capacity**. Each storage node monitors the throughput its replicas actually use. When a node crosses a threshold, an autoadmin service moves some replicas to other nodes, so flexible usage never piles up on one machine.
takeaway: Overbook on purpose, then watch real usage and move load before it hurts.
deeper:
**What rigid limits had going for them:** Under static per-partition caps, a node's worst-case load was known, because every partition had a hard ceiling. Bursting and table-level admission control removed that certainty by letting partitions use more than their original share. Good for customers, but a node can be oversubscribed if several of its partitions spike at once.

**The answer:** Accept overbooking and add active balancing. Nodes watch real consumption, and when one runs hot, autoadmin moves some of its replicas elsewhere.

**The whole arc:**
1. Static per-partition limits.
2. Bursting and adaptive capacity.
3. Table-level admission control.
4. Split for consumption.
5. Balancing consumed capacity.

**The lesson:** Per-partition limits cause throttling under skew. Table-level control plus consumption splits fix most skew, and balancing keeps nodes healthy. None of it fixes a single hot key.

quiz.q: A node hosts 20 replicas whose provisioned throughput sums to exactly its capacity. Five of them burst at once. What goes wrong, and what does DynamoDB do?
quiz.a: Actual use exceeds what the node can deliver, because bursting lets partitions exceed their provisioned share. The node crosses its threshold and autoadmin moves some replicas to other nodes.

mcq.q: What triggers DynamoDB's autoadmin to move replicas?
options: A storage node crossing a consumed-throughput threshold
A table exceeding its provisioned WCUs
A partition growing past its size limit
A client retrying a throttled request
mcq.why: Each node monitors its replicas' consumed throughput; when it crosses a threshold, autoadmin moves some replicas elsewhere.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: Splitting shards fixes most hot spots. What do you do when all the heat is on a single key?
title: You can't split a key: four defenses for one hot item
body: Splitting divides key ranges, and one key cannot be divided. So a single hot key needs other answers. **Caching** in front, such as memcache or a CDN for photos, is the main defense for reads. Read replicas spread the rest; Slicer can give hot slices more replicas. **Request coalescing**: Discord's Rust data service merges identical concurrent requests, so the database sees one query instead of thousands. For writes, **key salting** spreads one key across sub-keys.
takeaway: When you can't divide the key, divide or remove the requests.
deeper:
**Caching removes reads entirely:** A viral photo served from a CDN never reaches the storage node. That is why it is the main read defense.

**Replicas and coalescing:** Several servers holding the same data share the remaining reads, and Slicer's ability to give a hot slice more replicas automates this. Coalescing attacks duplication: when thousands of clients ask for the same thing at the same moment, most requests are redundant. Discord routes by channel ID with consistent hashing, so one instance sees them all, issues one database query and shares the result.

**Writes are the hard case:** Caches and read replicas do nothing for writes. Salting handles hot counters by spreading writes over sub-keys.

**Even DynamoDB agrees:** On its no-split path for a single hot key, the answer is to rely on admission control and caching.

quiz.q: A live-event page gets 50,000 reads per second for one record, and your database auto-splits aggressively. Latency is terrible. What's the first fix, and why won't splitting help?
quiz.a: Put a cache or CDN in front so repeated reads never reach storage. Splitting can't divide one key; the record stays on one shard however many times you split.

mcq.q: Which defense does Discord use against a single hot key?
options: Merging identical concurrent requests into one query
Splitting the hot key's shard into halves
Salting the channel ID into sub-keys
Moving the channel to a separate region
mcq.why: Discord's Rust data service coalesces identical concurrent requests, so the database sees one query instead of thousands.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: One video's like counter takes every write and pins one shard. How do you spread a single counter?
title: Key salting: split one hot counter into 16 sub-keys
body: Heavy writes to one key pin one shard. **Key salting** spreads them. Instead of one counter, `likes:video123`, the application writes to N sub-keys, `likes:video123:0` through `:15`, picking one per increment. The sub-keys hash to different shards, so writes spread across many servers. To read the total, the application reads all sub-keys and sums them. The catch: the application must know about the salting; the database won't do it for you.
takeaway: Salting trades one hot write for N cheap writes and one expensive read.
deeper:
**The payoff:** With 16 sub-keys, each shard sees roughly a sixteenth of the write load. The hot spot disappears as long as 16 servers can carry the total.

**Reads get costly:** One logical read now fans out to N sub-keys, multiplying read work and exposing every read to the slowest of N responses. Salting suits write-heavy, read-light data such as like counters, view counts or event tallies, and fits poorly on data read constantly.

**The application owns it:** Every writer and reader must use the same scheme and the same N, and changing N later needs care. A sum across sub-keys is not an atomic snapshot unless you add coordination.

**The broader rule:** Design keys so writes spread, with a hash prefix or randomized IDs, and cache hot reads, rather than hoping the database fixes hot keys itself.

quiz.q: You salt a counter into 16 sub-keys. Writes are fine, but the page that shows the count on every view gets slower. Why?
quiz.a: Each read now fetches and sums 16 sub-keys across shards, waiting on the slowest. Salting fits write-heavy, read-light data; cache the total for frequent reads.

mcq.q: What is the main cost of salting a hot counter into N sub-keys?
options: Every read must fetch and sum all N sub-keys
Writes must be coordinated across N shards
The database must support automatic salting
Each sub-key needs its own replica set
mcq.why: Writes spread over N shards, but a read fans out to all N and sums them, and the app must implement the scheme.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
hook: “Our database auto-splits, so hot spots are handled.” Which two kinds of hot spot does that sentence miss?
title: Auto-split fixes hot ranges, not hot keys or timestamps
body: Teams often assume that because the database auto-splits, hot spots are solved. **Auto-split** fixes hot ranges, where many keys in one range are busy. It cannot fix a single hot key, because one key cannot be divided. It cannot fix a monotonically increasing key like a timestamp, because each split leaves the newest range hot. The fix is design: shape keys so writes spread, with a hash prefix or randomized IDs, and cache hot reads.
takeaway: Auto-split is a feature for ranges, not an excuse for bad keys.
deeper:
**Why the belief spreads:** Auto-splitting is real and useful. DynamoDB's split-for-consumption handles hot ranges, with splits usually completing in minutes. Range-partitioned systems like Bigtable, Spanner and CockroachDB split ranges when they grow too large. It is easy to generalize that into 'the database handles all hot spots'.

**Even the best splitter gives up:** DynamoDB's paper says a single hot item or a sequentially accessed key range will not benefit from splitting. DynamoDB detects these patterns and deliberately avoids useless splits.

**So it lands on key design:** Avoid monotonically increasing values as the leading part of a key; prefix a hash or use random IDs. For hot individual items, plan caching, read replicas, request coalescing or salting from the start.

**Ask this:** Which keys could become hot, like a celebrity, a viral item or the current time bucket, and what happens when they do?

quiz.q: An orders table uses an auto-incrementing order_id as its range key on a database that auto-splits. Writes still bottleneck on one node. Why, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Every new ID sorts after the rest, so after each split the newest range takes all writes. Use a hashed prefix or random IDs so writes spread.

mcq.q: Which hot spot can database auto-splitting actually fix?
options: A range where many different keys are busy
A single key read by millions of users
A key that always increases, like a timestamp
A counter incremented on every like
mcq.why: Splitting divides a range among servers. A single key can't be divided, and increasing keys keep the newest range hot.

hook: Data nodes scale by adding disks. Why does the metadata tier need a whole sharded database of its own?
title: Put metadata in a sharded database, not one server's RAM
body: The data plane scales by adding disks. The metadata plane is harder: it needs consistency, and its access is skewed. Two lessons follow. First, keep metadata in a scalable database, not one server's memory: Colossus stores it in Bigtable, and Meta's Tectonic in ZippyDB, a sharded key-value store. Second, **hash-partition** metadata. Tectonic splits it into name, file and block layers and hash-partitions each; the paper says this effectively avoids hotspots in the metadata layer.
takeaway: Metadata is a database problem. Treat it like one, then shard it.
deeper:
**The single-server ceiling:** Keeping all metadata in one machine's memory, as HDFS did, caps the number of files at what that memory holds and makes that server a throughput bottleneck. A sharded database removes both limits: capacity and throughput grow with its shard count.

**Tectonic's layers:** Roughly, the name layer maps paths and directories to files, the file layer maps files to blocks, and the block layer tracks where blocks are stored. Each layer is hash-partitioned independently.

**Why hash, not range:** Metadata access is skewed toward popular files and directories. A range-partitioned namespace would put a busy directory and all its children on one shard. Hashing spreads that load.

**The price:** The usual one for hashing. Operations that walk a directory in order, or touch many related entries, may need to visit several shards.

quiz.q: Your file system's namespace is range-partitioned by path, and a popular /shared/models directory keeps one metadata shard at 100 percent. What would Tectonic do differently?
quiz.a: Hash-partition each metadata layer so entries under a busy directory scatter across shards instead of sitting together; Tectonic's paper says this effectively avoids metadata hotspots.

mcq.q: Where does Tectonic store its metadata?
options: In ZippyDB, a sharded key-value store
In one metadata server's memory
In Bigtable, like Colossus does
In a file on each storage node
mcq.why: Tectonic keeps metadata in ZippyDB and hash-partitions its name, file and block layers; Colossus is the one using Bigtable.

hook: One Meta storage cluster ran on 4,208 nodes. How many metadata items did it have to keep track of?
title: 10.7 billion files in one cluster: size metadata by count
body: Petabytes are only half a sizing question. A representative Tectonic cluster in 2021 had 1,590 PB capacity, 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks, on 4,208 storage nodes. That is billions of metadata items in one cluster. Whatever holds that metadata must be sized for the number of items it tracks, not the petabytes, because every file and block is an entry to store, index and look up.

stat.label: files in one Tectonic cluster, plus 15B blocks

takeaway: Ask how many things, not just how many bytes.
deeper:
**The mismatch:** A few thousand storage nodes serve the petabytes, since each holds many large drives. The metadata system must track tens of billions of entries across files and blocks, and reads and writes touch them constantly. A metadata tier sized by bytes would be hopelessly small for the entry count.

**A fill-level footnote:** The same snapshot shows headroom. 1,250 PB used of 1,590 PB works out to about 79 percent full, though the cluster is elsewhere described as about 70 percent full, so treat the exact figure with care.

**Count is its own dimension:** Object count breaks index size, memory per object and directory size, separately from capacity. It is also why grouping matters: Ceph tracks placement groups rather than individual objects.

**The ask:** When planning, get expected files and blocks, then size the metadata tier for that number.

quiz.q: A capacity plan sizes the metadata tier at one node per 5 PB stored. For a cluster like this Tectonic one, what's wrong with that rule?
quiz.a: Metadata load follows item count, not bytes. That cluster held 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks; a byte-based rule ignores how many entries must be stored and looked up.

mcq.q: What did a representative 2021 Tectonic cluster hold?
options: 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks
10.7 million files and 15 million blocks
1.07 billion files and 1.5 billion blocks
107 billion files and 150 billion blocks
mcq.why: The FAST 2021 paper's cluster: 1,590 PB capacity, 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files, 15 billion blocks, 4,208 storage nodes.

predict.q: A 2021 Meta Tectonic cluster ran on 4,208 storage nodes. About how many files did it hold?
options: About 10.7 billion
About 10.7 million
About 1 trillion

hook: Sharing one storage cluster across teams saves a fortune. So why do the teams end up fighting over it?
title: Multi-tenancy: one team's idle capacity, another's peak
body: A **tenant** is a user of the storage system with its own identity, quota and expectations: a team, an application or an external customer. Multi-tenancy means many tenants share the same hardware. It saves huge amounts of money, because one team's idle capacity serves another team's peak. But it creates the **noisy neighbor** problem: one tenant's burst, like a large batch job, hurts everyone else's latency on the shared machines.
takeaway: Sharing turns idle capacity into savings and every burst into everyone's problem.
deeper:
**The aggregation effect, organized:** Independent demands peak at different times, so a shared pool needs less hardware than separate pools each sized for its own peak. In a 1-billion-user app, search, ads and ML share one cluster, and the savings are large.

**The other side of the coin:** The same disks, network links and metadata servers serve everyone. A background analytics scan can fill disk queues that a user-facing service depends on. Because tenants have different owners and priorities, the problem is as much organizational as technical.

**The toolbox:** Quotas, token-bucket admission control, priority classes with fair scheduling, and physical isolation for the largest tenants, plus explicit decisions about which resources are guaranteed and which are best-effort.

**The catch:** Every saving from sharing is borrowed against the isolation you build. Skip the isolation and the savings come back as incidents.

quiz.q: The ML team's nightly scan makes the ads team's p99 read latency jump, on a shared cluster with plenty of free space. What's this called, and why doesn't free space help?
quiz.a: The noisy neighbor problem. The scan consumes shared IOPS and queues, not bytes, so free capacity does nothing; you need admission control or priority scheduling.

mcq.q: Why does multi-tenancy save money?
options: One tenant's idle capacity can serve another's peak
Tenants share encryption keys and metadata
Each tenant gets dedicated, smaller hardware
Shared clusters need no replication at all
mcq.why: Independent tenants peak at different times, so a shared pool needs less hardware than separate pools sized for each peak.

hook: One tenant suddenly sends 10× its usual traffic. What stops it from wrecking everyone else's latency?
title: Four tools that keep tenants from hurting each other
body: Storage systems isolate tenants with four main tools. **Quotas** set hard limits on bytes, objects or request rate. Admission control with **token buckets** limits rates: tokens refill at a fixed rate, each request takes one, and an empty bucket means reject or delay. Priority classes and fair scheduling at each storage node decide whose request goes first under contention. Physical isolation, separate clusters or cells, is saved for the biggest or most sensitive tenants.
takeaway: Cap the slow-changing, schedule the contended, and wall off only the giants.
deeper:
**Different speeds, different tools:** Quotas are coarse and slow-changing, suited to capacity. Token buckets handle rates, allowing short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-run average. DynamoDB's global admission control is built on table-level token buckets, with partition-level buckets as defense in depth.

**The moment of contention:** When a disk queue is full, a scheduler decides whose request runs next. Without one, whoever sends the most requests wins. Tectonic's weighted round-robin with Gold, Silver and Bronze classes is the worked example.

**The expensive option:** Separate clusters or cells eliminate interference but give up the pooling savings that motivated sharing in the first place. That is why they are reserved for tenants large enough to justify their own hardware or sensitive enough that sharing is unacceptable.

**In practice:** Most systems combine several of these.

quiz.q: A tenant's token bucket refills at 100 tokens per second and holds 500. It's been idle, then sends 800 requests in one second. What happens?
quiz.a: About 500 are admitted from saved tokens, plus roughly 100 refilled that second; the rest are rejected or delayed. Buckets allow short bursts but cap the average rate.

mcq.q: When is physical isolation (separate clusters or cells) the right tool?
options: For the biggest or most sensitive tenants
For every tenant, as the default
For tenants with bursty request rates
For tenants that store only cold data
mcq.why: Separate clusters remove interference but lose pooling savings, so they're reserved for tenants big or sensitive enough to justify it.

hook: Meta's Tectonic gives each tenant fixed disk space but pools its IOPS. Why treat the two differently?
title: Tectonic reserves capacity but shares IOPS
body: Meta's Tectonic (FAST 2021) splits resources into two kinds. **Non-ephemeral** resources, mainly storage capacity, change slowly and, once given to a tenant, cannot be shared: bytes on disk belong to someone. Quotas manage them. **Ephemeral** resources, like storage IOPS and metadata query capacity, have demand that changes quickly. These must be shared dynamically, because static reservations would leave most of them idle while other tenants starve.
takeaway: Reserve what can't be shared. Pool what vanishes if unused.
deeper:
**Capacity is exclusive:** If tenant A stores a petabyte, that space is taken until A deletes it. No scheduling lets tenant B use it meanwhile. So a quota, a fixed allocation that changes on planning timescales, fits.

**IOPS are perishable:** An IOPS not used this second is gone forever, and a tenant's demand can swing quickly. Carving IOPS into fixed per-tenant slices would waste most of the fleet's performance, the same waste static sharding and DynamoDB's per-partition limits suffered.

**The hybrid:** Each tenant gets a guaranteed quota of ephemeral resources, so it can count on a baseline. Unused ephemeral capacity is then redistributed, first within the tenant by traffic class, then to other tenants.

**The payoff:** Predictability from the guarantee, efficiency from the pooling. Neither pure reservation nor pure sharing gets both.

quiz.q: A proposal gives every tenant a fixed, reserved slice of cluster IOPS, just like disk quotas. Using Tectonic's reasoning, what's the flaw?
quiz.a: IOPS are ephemeral: unused IOPS vanish each second and demand swings fast, so fixed slices sit idle while others starve. Guarantee a baseline, then share spare IOPS dynamically.

mcq.q: How does Tectonic classify storage IOPS?
options: Ephemeral, shared dynamically
Non-ephemeral, managed by quotas
Ephemeral, never shared across tenants
Non-ephemeral, shared by class
mcq.why: IOPS and metadata query capacity change quickly, so Tectonic treats them as ephemeral and shares them dynamically on top of guarantees.

hook: A background job and a user request hit the same busy Tectonic disk. How does the user request go first?
title: Gold, Silver, Bronze: how Tectonic ranks traffic
body: Inside each Tectonic tenant, applications are grouped into about 50 **TrafficGroups** per cluster, each with a **TrafficClass**: Gold for latency-sensitive, Silver for normal, Bronze for background. Each tenant gets a guaranteed quota of ephemeral resources. Spare capacity goes first to the tenant's own TrafficGroups by class, then to other tenants. Storage nodes run weighted round-robin that skips a group's turn if it would exceed its limit, and lets lower classes yield to Gold.
takeaway: Guarantee a floor, share the surplus, and let urgent work cut the line.
deeper:
**A manageable unit:** Instead of tracking many applications separately, Tectonic tracks about 50 groups per cluster, each with a class encoding how urgent its requests are.

**Who gets the spare:** A tenant's unused guarantee benefits its own groups first, in class order, so its Gold work is covered before its Bronze. Only then does leftover capacity flow to other tenants. That rewards tenants for their guarantee while keeping the fleet busy.

**On each node:** Weighted round-robin serves groups in turn by weight, but skips a group whose next request would push it over its limit, so a greedy group cannot monopolize the disk. The yielding optimization lets a Bronze or Silver request step aside when a Gold request is waiting.

**Also a tail-latency tool:** Running background work like compaction and repair at a lower class keeps it from creating slow responses for latency-sensitive traffic.

quiz.q: Tenant X has unused guaranteed IOPS. Its own Bronze backfill job and another tenant's Gold service both want them. Who gets them first?
quiz.a: Tenant X's own TrafficGroups, by class, including its Bronze job. Spare capacity goes to the tenant's own groups first, and only leftovers flow to other tenants.

mcq.q: What does Tectonic's scheduler do when a TrafficGroup would exceed its limit?
options: Skips that group's turn in the round-robin
Queues its requests until the next hour
Upgrades it to Gold temporarily
Moves the group to another cluster
mcq.why: Storage nodes use weighted round-robin that skips any TrafficGroup whose request would exceed its limit, so no group monopolizes the disk.

hook: Meta moved its data warehouse onto the same clusters as blob storage. What happened to its cluster count?
title: Shared Tectonic clusters cut warehouse clusters by 10×
body: Isolation machinery is expensive to build. Tectonic's payoff shows why it's worth it. Consolidating blob storage and the data warehouse onto shared clusters cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10×, and the warehouse absorbed traffic spikes using blob storage's spare IOPS. DynamoDB faces the same tension publicly: nodes host thousands of replicas from unrelated customers, so it caps **partition-level** token buckets so no one application takes a significant share of a node.

stat.label: fewer warehouse clusters on shared Tectonic

takeaway: Sharing pays only as well as you enforce it.
deeper:
**Complementary tenants:** Blob storage holds huge volumes with IOPS to spare. Warehouse workloads are spiky. Once they share clusters with guaranteed quotas and traffic classes, the warehouse's spikes land on capacity that would otherwise sit idle in blob storage.

**A harder setting:** Meta's tenants are internal teams who can negotiate. DynamoDB's tenants are external customers who never see each other and expect predictable performance. Global admission control gives each customer flexibility across its own partitions, but the partition-level cap exists so one customer's hot partition cannot take over a node shared with thousands of other customers' replicas.

**The common thread:** In both cases, savings depend on enforcement. Without quotas, scheduling and caps, consolidation would become a stream of noisy-neighbor incidents instead of a 10× efficiency gain.

quiz.q: DynamoDB already enforces table-level limits through GAC. Why keep a partition-level cap at all?
quiz.a: Storage nodes host thousands of replicas from unrelated customers. The cap stops one application's hot partition from consuming all or a significant share of a node's resources.

mcq.q: How did the warehouse absorb traffic spikes after moving onto shared Tectonic clusters?
options: By using blob storage's spare IOPS
By buying dedicated flash for spikes
By delaying spikes to off-peak hours
By compressing warehouse data further
mcq.why: Blob storage and the warehouse shared clusters, so warehouse spikes drew on blob storage's otherwise idle IOPS.

predict.q: Meta moved blob storage and its data warehouse onto shared Tectonic clusters. Warehouse cluster count:
options: Fell by 10×
Fell by about 10 percent
Stayed about the same

hook: A batch job slows a user-facing service on a shared cluster. Why does that become a fight, not a ticket?
title: Multi-tenancy is economics with a reliability bill
body: Multi-tenancy is an economic decision with a reliability cost. Before sharing a cluster, get answers. What is the **isolation unit**: tenant, application or request class? Which resources are guaranteed, and which are best-effort? What happens to a Gold request when the cluster is full of Bronze work? Who pays for headroom? If nobody can answer, the shared cluster becomes a political problem the first time a batch job hurts a user-facing service.
takeaway: Write down who gets hurt first before the first batch job decides for you.
deeper:
**An agreement, not a feature:** The savings are real, as Tectonic's 10× consolidation shows, but they come from people sharing resources they would otherwise control alone. When something breaks, the questions become who caused it, whose work should have been protected, and who should have paid to prevent it.

**Each question maps to a design choice:**
1. Isolation unit: Tectonic's TrafficGroups, DynamoDB's tables and partitions.
2. Guaranteed versus best-effort: Tectonic's guaranteed ephemeral quotas versus redistributed spare capacity.
3. Gold versus Bronze: weighted round-robin with yielding.
4. Headroom: someone must fund spare capacity so bursts and repairs don't hurt guaranteed tenants.

**Why it goes political:** Without written answers, the first incident becomes an argument about blame and priority instead of a quick application of agreed policy.

quiz.q: You're asked to approve putting the analytics team on the same cluster as checkout. Which four questions do you want answered first?
quiz.a: What the isolation unit is; which resources are guaranteed versus best-effort; what happens to Gold requests when Bronze work fills the cluster; and who pays for headroom.

mcq.q: What happens if a shared cluster has no agreed isolation rules?
options: The first batch-job incident becomes a political fight
The cluster automatically falls back to fair sharing
Tenants are moved to separate cells by default
Quotas are derived from past usage automatically
mcq.why: Without agreed answers, a batch job hurting a user-facing service turns into an argument over blame and priority.

hook: Your global database has flawless code. Why is there still a hard floor under every strongly consistent write?
title: 70-80 ms: the speed-of-light floor under global writes
body: A 1-billion-user app has users on every continent. Light in fiber needs roughly 70-80 ms for a round trip between the US East Coast and Western Europe, an assumption based on typical published figures. A **strongly consistent write** that must reach a quorum across continents cannot finish faster than that, however good the software. So every multi-region design decides which operations pay that round trip and which stay local.

stat.label: round trip, US East Coast to Western Europe

takeaway: Software can't beat physics. It can only choose who pays for it.
deeper:
**A floor, not an estimate:** Real round trips add routing, queuing and processing, so they are longer. Consensus protocols may need more than one round trip per write. If a write must be acknowledged on two continents, it takes at least one intercontinental round trip.

**The toolbox for living with it:** Asynchronous replication keeps writes local and pays with possible loss and conflicts. Synchronous replication pays the round trip for no data loss and strong consistency. Leader placement puts the write-ordering replica near the writers. Akkio-style migration moves data to follow users. Last-writer-wins, vector clocks and CRDTs handle concurrent async writes, and home regions avoid conflicts.

**Law on top of physics:** Data residency rules mean some data cannot simply go wherever latency is best.

quiz.q: A product manager wants strongly consistent writes to a quorum spanning Virginia and Frankfurt, with a 20 ms median write target. What do you tell them?
quiz.a: Impossible: a US East to Western Europe round trip is roughly 70-80 ms, a floor any cross-continent quorum write must pay. Relax consistency, go async, or keep the quorum in one region.

mcq.q: Why can't a strongly consistent cross-continent quorum write beat roughly 70-80 ms?
options: Light in fiber needs that long for the round trip
Consensus software adds that much CPU time
Disks need that long to persist each write
Regions batch writes into 70 ms windows
mcq.why: The quorum spans continents, and light in fiber needs roughly 70-80 ms for a US East Coast to Western Europe round trip.

hook: A region goes dark mid-write. One design lost nothing, another lost its last few seconds. What did each trade?
title: Sync or async: pay in write latency or in lost writes
body: **Synchronous replication** acknowledges a write only after a quorum in multiple regions has it: every write pays a cross-region round trip, but a region failure loses nothing (RPO = 0) and strong consistency is possible, as in Spanner multi-region and Physalia-style designs. **Asynchronous replication** acknowledges once the local region has it: latency stays local, but recent writes can be lost and consistency is eventual, with possible conflicts. Examples: DynamoDB global tables, Cassandra multi-DC with local quorum, most blob geo-replication.
takeaway: Pick your pain per dataset: slow writes or a nonzero RPO.
deeper:
**Two terms:** RPO, recovery point objective, is how much recent data you can lose. RTO, recovery time objective, is how long you can be down. Synchronous replication reaches RPO = 0 because nothing is acknowledged until it exists in several regions. Async has a nonzero RPO: writes acknowledged locally but not yet shipped die with the region.

**Consistency splits the same way:** With synchronous quorums, a read can be guaranteed to see the latest write. With async, other regions lag, and if two regions accept writes to the same item concurrently, the conflict must be resolved later.

**Mixing is normal:** Synchronous suits small, critical records like metadata. Asynchronous suits bulk data like photos and logs, where a little possible loss or staleness is acceptable for local write speed.

**The one-line version:** Multi-region design is a choice between write latency and data loss.

quiz.q: A payments ledger and a photo store both need multi-region copies. Which replication mode would you pick for each, and what does each cost?
quiz.a: Synchronous for the ledger: RPO = 0 and strong consistency, at a cross-region round trip per write. Asynchronous for photos: local-speed writes, accepting that recent uploads may be lost in a region failure.

mcq.q: What is the RPO of synchronous multi-region replication on a region failure?
options: Zero: no acknowledged write is lost
A few seconds of recent writes
Equal to the cross-region round trip
The time until failover completes
mcq.why: Writes are acknowledged only after a quorum in multiple regions has them, so losing one region loses no acknowledged data.

hook: Spanner spreads replicas across regions. Why does Google still tell you to run your writers near just one?
title: Spanner: put write-heavy compute near the default leader
body: Many strongly consistent systems have a leader per shard that orders writes, so where it lives sets write latency. Google Spanner makes this explicit. A regional configuration has three read-write replicas in different zones of one region. Multi-region configurations spread read-write replicas across regions, plus a **witness region** that votes but holds no full data copy. Each has a **default leader region** that handles writes, and Google advises placing write-heavy compute within or close to it.
takeaway: Writes travel to the leader. Put the writers where the leader lives.
deeper:
**Why the advice:** Every write goes through the shard's leader. A writer far from the leader pays a long round trip on every write before consensus even starts. Placing application servers in or near the default leader region keeps that hop short.

**The witness trick:** A witness region provides a vote across regions without the cost of another full data copy. It takes part in consensus, helping tolerate a regional failure, but doesn't store all the data.

**Google's own framing:** Multi-region gives faster reads in more places at the cost of a small increase in write latency. Reads can come from nearby replicas; writes need agreement across regions.

**Residency angle:** Spanner also offers dual-region configurations that keep all replicas inside one country for data residency, so a region can fail over without data leaving the permitted jurisdiction.

quiz.q: Your Spanner multi-region instance has its default leader in the US, but your write-heavy service runs in Europe. Writes are slow. Why, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Every write goes to the leader, so each one crosses the Atlantic before consensus starts. Move the write-heavy compute into or near the default leader region.

mcq.q: What does a Spanner witness region do?
options: Votes in consensus without a full data copy
Serves all reads for the nearest users
Handles writes when the leader is busy
Stores backups outside the main regions
mcq.why: A witness region votes but holds no full copy, giving a cross-region majority without paying for another full replica.

hook: A user moves from London to Singapore. Should their data stay behind in the old datacenter?
title: Akkio moves each user's data to where it's used
body: A fixed leader region makes distant users pay. A smarter approach moves the data. Meta's Akkio (OSDI 2018) groups related data into **u-shards**, for example one user's data, and migrates them between datacenters to follow access. Compared with reasonable alternatives, the paper reports up to 50 percent lower access latency, up to 50 percent less cross-datacenter traffic and up to 40 percent less storage, managing over 100 PB in production.

stat.label: lower access latency, at best, vs alternatives

takeaway: Move the small thing people use together, not the big thing you sharded by.
deeper:
**The right unit:** Akkio's insight is that locality belongs to a group of data accessed together, not to a database shard. A u-shard, such as one user's data, is small enough to move cheaply and coherent enough that moving it makes all related accesses local. A database shard mixes many users in many places, so no single location suits all of them.

**Where the gains plausibly come from:** Lower latency from serving users nearby. Less cross-datacenter traffic from not fetching remote data on every access. Less storage from not keeping a full copy of everyone's data everywhere. The paper compares against what it calls reasonable alternatives.

**It fits a pattern:** Movable, directory-style placement beats fixed placement at scale, and Shard Manager found most applications need geo-distribution.

**Pairs with home regions:** A user's data has a home, and Akkio lets that home move with the user.

quiz.q: Your database is sharded by user_id hash, and each shard holds users from every continent. Why can't you just move a shard closer to its users, and what did Akkio do instead?
quiz.a: Each shard's users are everywhere, so no location suits them all. Akkio groups each user's related data into a small u-shard and migrates that to where it's accessed.

mcq.q: What is an Akkio u-shard?
options: A group of related data, like one user's
A full database shard in one datacenter
A replica kept only for disaster recovery
A cache entry for frequently read keys
mcq.why: Akkio groups data accessed together, such as one user's data, into u-shards that migrate between datacenters to follow access.

predict.q: Akkio migrates each user's data to the datacenter that accesses it. Best reported cut in access latency?
options: Up to 50 percent
Up to 5 percent
Up to 95 percent

hook: Two regions update the same record a moment apart. The later update vanishes, with no error. How?
title: Last-writer-wins is simple, popular, and silently lossy
body: With asynchronous multi-region writes, two regions can update the same item at once, and the system must pick a result. **Last-writer-wins** (LWW) attaches a timestamp to each write and keeps the latest. It is simple and widely used, in Cassandra's per-column timestamps and DynamoDB global tables. The costs: with **clock skew**, a write that truly came later can carry an earlier timestamp and silently lose. And if the unit is a whole item, concurrent updates to different fields overwrite each other.
takeaway: LWW doesn't keep the last write. It keeps the biggest timestamp.
deeper:
**Why it's the default:** LWW needs no coordination and no application logic. Every replica applies the same rule and converges on the same value.

**Cost 1, clocks:** Machines' clocks drift, so timestamps from two regions are not perfectly comparable. If region A's clock runs slightly fast, its writes win even when region B wrote afterward. The losing write disappears without an error, which makes these bugs hard to notice.

**Cost 2, granularity:** A user changes their display name in one region and their photo in another. If the whole profile is one unit, one change is lost though they touched different fields. Cassandra's per-column timestamps let concurrent updates to different columns both survive.

**Where it fits:** Fine when overwrites are acceptable, like a latest-status field. Poor when every write matters, like counters or carts, where merge-based types or single-writer designs are better.

quiz.q: A user edits their bio in Europe at 10:00:00.200, then again from the US at 10:00:00.500, but the US server's clock is 400 ms slow. Under LWW, which edit survives?
quiz.a: The European edit. The US write is stamped about 10:00:00.100, earlier than 10:00:00.200, so LWW silently discards the truly later write.

mcq.q: How can last-writer-wins lose a write that really happened later?
options: Clock skew gives it an earlier timestamp
Its region failed before replicating it
It was written with a weaker quorum
Its item exceeded the size limit
mcq.why: LWW keeps the highest timestamp, so a skewed clock can stamp a later write as earlier and it silently loses.

hook: Two regions each add an item to the same shopping cart at the same moment. How do you keep both items?
title: Dynamo kept both versions and let the app merge them
body: Last-writer-wins would silently drop one of the two cart updates. The Dynamo paper (2007) took another path: use **vector clocks** to detect that two versions were written concurrently, keep both, and let the application merge them. For a shopping cart, the app merges both carts so neither item is lost. It is powerful, because no write is silently discarded. The cost: it pushes complexity onto developers, who must write correct merge logic for every data type.
takeaway: Dynamo refused to guess, so every developer had to.
deeper:
**How vector clocks decide:** A vector clock tracks, per replica, how many updates a version has seen. Comparing two tells the system whether one version descends from the other, so the newer simply replaces it, or whether they were written independently, a true conflict. Unlike LWW, this does not depend on synchronized wall clocks.

**On a true conflict:** The application gets both versions and decides how to combine them. For a cart, taking the union of items is sensible, though it can bring back an item the user deleted in one region.

**The burden:** Every application must handle conflicts correctly for every kind of data it stores, and bugs in merge logic corrupt data.

**Where others went:** Many later systems chose simpler LWW semantics, CRDTs that bake a well-defined merge into the data type, or single-writer home regions that avoid conflicts entirely.

quiz.q: Under Dynamo-style versioning, a user removes a book from their cart in one region while adding a pen in another. After a union merge, what might the cart contain, and why?
quiz.a: Both the pen and the removed book. The union keeps every item seen in either version, so a deletion in one version can be undone by the other.

mcq.q: What does Dynamo do when vector clocks show two concurrent versions?
options: Keeps both and lets the application merge
Keeps the one with the newer timestamp
Rejects the second write with an error
Averages the two values automatically
mcq.why: Dynamo detects true conflicts with vector clocks, keeps both versions, and hands them to the application to merge.

hook: A like counter takes writes in five regions at once, with no coordination. Why do all replicas still agree?
title: CRDTs: data types built so every merge is well-defined
body: Hand-written merge logic is a bug magnet. **CRDTs** (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are data types designed so merges are always well-defined and all replicas converge, whatever order updates arrive in: counters, sets, maps, registers. They suit likes counters, presence and collaborative edits, where many regions update at once. The limit: not every business rule can be a CRDT. A rule like 'balance must not go below zero' needs coordination.
takeaway: CRDTs make merging safe. They can't enforce a rule about the global total.
deeper:
**Merge lives in the type:** A counter CRDT can track increments per region and sum them, so concurrent increments in different regions never overwrite each other and every replica eventually reports the same total. Because convergence is built in, replicas accept writes locally with no coordination and still agree once updates propagate.

**Good fits:** Likes, view counts, online-presence flags and collaborative documents. All have many concurrent writers and tolerate brief disagreement between regions.

**The boundary:** Invariants over global state. Two regions could each approve a withdrawal that is valid locally and together overdraw the account. Enforcing 'never below zero' needs coordination, such as a single owner or a synchronous consensus step, which brings back the cross-region latency CRDTs avoid.

**The lesson:** CRDTs are a tool for the right data, not a universal answer to multi-region consistency.

quiz.q: A wallet holds $100. Region A approves a $70 withdrawal while region B approves $60, both locally valid. Why can't a CRDT prevent the overdraft?
quiz.a: 'Never below zero' depends on global state, and each region decided alone; the merge converges on -$30. Enforcing the rule needs coordination, like a single owner or a consensus step.

mcq.q: Which requirement can a CRDT not enforce by itself?
options: An account balance must never go below zero
A like count must reflect every increment
A set must contain every item ever added
All replicas must converge to one value
mcq.why: CRDTs merge concurrent updates safely, but a global invariant like a non-negative balance needs coordination across regions.

hook: The easiest write conflict to resolve is one that never happens. How do you make that the default?
title: Home regions: one writer per key means nothing to merge
body: LWW, vector clocks and CRDTs all clean up conflicts after they happen. The simplest approach avoids them. Give each item a **home region** that owns all writes to it, a single writer per key, and replicate asynchronously elsewhere for reads. Because only one region ever accepts writes for an item, two regions can never update it concurrently. This is very common for user data: your profile is written in your home region and read from replicas everywhere.
takeaway: One writer per key: no clocks to trust, no merges to write.
deeper:
**The trade:** A user who travels far from home pays a cross-region round trip on writes, since writes must go home. Reads stay fast everywhere because async replicas serve them locally, though they may be slightly stale.

**Why it suits user data:** Users mostly stay near home, their data is mostly written by themselves, and slightly stale reads by others are acceptable.

**What it needs:** A router that knows each user's home region. An EU user's profile write goes to a router that reads the user's home region and sends the write to the EU leader region.

**How it combines:** Akkio shows the home can move when a user relocates. Residency rules can be enforced by choosing the home by jurisdiction. And because writes are ordered in one place, apps avoid LWW's clock-skew risk and vector clocks' merge burden.

quiz.q: A US-homed user travels to Tokyo and updates their profile. Where does the write go, what does it cost, and why is there no conflict risk?
quiz.a: It goes to the US home region, paying a trans-Pacific round trip. Only the home region accepts writes for that key, so no other region can write it concurrently.

mcq.q: How does a home region per item avoid write conflicts?
options: Only that region accepts writes for the item
It stamps writes with synchronized clocks
It merges concurrent writes with a CRDT
It locks the item in every region first
mcq.why: Single writer per key means concurrent cross-region updates to one item never happen; other regions just serve async read replicas.

hook: A law says EU data stays in the EU. Where in your storage stack does that sentence actually get enforced?
title: Data residency is a placement constraint, not a policy doc
body: **Data residency** laws, such as rules in the EU, India or China, may require certain data to be stored or processed inside a country or region. In a storage system that becomes a hard placement constraint. The shard manager or placement layer must know each shard's jurisdiction and refuse illegal placements. Backups, logs, caches and analytics copies are copies too. Failover targets must stay inside the allowed area.
takeaway: If placement doesn't know the law, placement will eventually break it.
deeper:
**One write, traced:**
1. An EU user writes their profile under a policy of residency = EU.
2. The router reads the user's home region and sends the write to the EU leader region.
3. A synchronous quorum replicates inside EU zones, and backups are stored in the EU only.
4. A US read replica gets an asynchronous stream of allowed fields only.

**Field-level residency:** That last step shows some parts of a record may leave the region while personal data does not.

**Encode it where decisions happen:** Shard managers like Meta's already accept constraints such as keeping a shard near its users. Jurisdiction is the same kind of constraint, except it must never be traded away for load or cost.

**The easy miss, failover:** A disaster plan that fails EU data over to a US region breaks the law exactly when everyone is busy. Spanner's dual-region configurations exist so a region can fail without data leaving the country.

quiz.q: Your placement layer spreads replicas purely by load and free space, and legal reviews a policy doc once a year. EU residency applies. What will eventually go wrong?
quiz.a: Load balancing or failover will put an EU shard, backup or replica outside the EU. The placement layer must know each shard's jurisdiction and refuse illegal placements automatically.

mcq.q: Why do Spanner dual-region configurations exist?
options: To fail over while keeping replicas in one country
To halve write latency for global users
To store backups on a second continent
To add a witness region for cheap votes
mcq.why: Failover targets must stay inside the allowed area; dual-region configurations keep every replica within one country for residency.

hook: Your EU customer table never leaves the EU. How can that customer's personal data still end up abroad?
title: Residency enforced only in the primary database leaks
body: A common mistake is enforcing data residency only in the primary database. The main tables stay in the EU, but a debug log, an analytics export or a cross-region backup quietly copies personal data abroad. Each of those is a copy, and the rule applies to copies. Residency must be a **property of the data**, carried with it and enforced on every copy path, not a setting on one database.
takeaway: The law follows the bytes, not the database they started in.
deeper:
**Copies multiply:** Application logs capture request payloads. Analytics pipelines export tables to a central warehouse, often in one region. Caches sit near users worldwide. Backups travel to a distant region for disaster recovery. Cross-region read replicas serve users elsewhere. Failover replicas wait in case of an outage. Each path can move EU personal data out without anyone touching the primary.

**Making it a property:** Tag data with its jurisdiction, and make every pipeline, backup job, cache and replication stream respect the tag. In a residency-aware design, the async stream to a US read replica carries allowed fields only, and backups are stored in the EU only.

**Audit the paths:** Trace every route data can take, not just where the primary copy sits. Backups, logs, caches, analytics exports, failover replicas and cross-region read replicas all belong on the checklist.

quiz.q: An audit confirms your EU user table lives only in EU regions. Name three places the same personal data might still sit outside the EU.
quiz.a: Any three of: backups, application or debug logs, caches, analytics exports, failover replicas, cross-region read replicas.

mcq.q: What is the core fix for residency leaks through logs and exports?
options: Treat residency as a property enforced on every copy
Move the primary database to a stricter region
Encrypt the primary database at rest
Delete application logs after 24 hours
mcq.why: Leaks come through secondary copies, so residency must travel with the data and be enforced wherever it is copied.

hook: Your cluster will be full in four months. Why might it already be too late to order more hardware?
title: Capacity planning: buy months before you need it
body: **Capacity planning** means predicting how much storage, IOPS, network and power you will need, and buying it before you need it. Two things make it hard. Lead times are long: servers need purchasing, shipping, racking and burn-in, and new datacenter space needs power and cooling built; in general industry experience, servers take months and buildings take years. And demand is lumpy: a launch or a new ML dataset can add petabytes in weeks, and data rarely shrinks.
takeaway: You're always buying for a future you have to guess.
deeper:
**Why the combination bites:** If demand were smooth and hardware arrived in days, you could buy as you go. Instead you commit money months or years ahead on a forecast that can be wrong either way. Underbuy and you run out of room. Overbuy and expensive hardware sits idle.

**Honest uncertainty:** Exact lead times are rarely published, so the numbers stay general: months for servers, years for buildings. Burn-in, running new hardware under load before trusting it with data, adds time even after machines arrive.

**Lumpiness beats trend lines:** One new ML training dataset or a launch that stores video can add petabytes quickly. Because data rarely shrinks, every spike becomes a permanent step up in the baseline.

**Hence the buffer:** Plans cover both the steady trend and sudden jumps, which is why a basic capacity model adds a safety buffer for forecast error on top of expected growth.

quiz.q: Your storage grows a steady 2 percent a month, until an ML team announces a new training dataset next quarter. Why does that break a simple trend-line plan?
quiz.a: Demand is lumpy: one dataset can add petabytes in weeks, and data rarely shrinks. With months of hardware lead time, the plan needs a buffer beyond the trend.

mcq.q: What two factors make storage capacity planning hard?
options: Long lead times and lumpy demand
High disk failure rates and slow repair
Expensive flash and cheap hard drives
Frequent upgrades and planned restarts
mcq.why: Hardware takes months (buildings, years) to arrive, while launches and datasets can add petabytes in weeks and data rarely shrinks.

hook: You have 100 PB, growing 3% a month, and hardware takes 6 months. How much should be installed when it lands?
title: 100 PB at 3% a month needs about 149 PB in 6 months
body: A teaching model, all assumptions: 100 PB used, 3 percent monthly growth, 6-month lead time. In 6 months, usage ≈ 100 × 1.03^6 ≈ 119 PB. With a **target maximum fill** of 80 percent, you need about 119 / 0.8 ≈ 149 PB of usable capacity installed by then. Then add a safety buffer for forecast error, say another month or two of growth.

stat.label: needed in 6 months, from 100 PB today

takeaway: Plan for the data you'll have when hardware lands, divided by safe fullness.
deeper:
**Step 1, compound over the lead time:** The question is how much data you will hold when hardware ordered today arrives. Growth compounds: 3 percent monthly over 6 months is about 19 percent, not 18.

**Step 2, divide by target fill:** This turns expected usage into required capacity. The 80 percent target reserves free space for repair, rebalancing and bursts. Skip the division and you are planning to be 100 percent full, which in distributed storage is dangerous.

**Step 3, add a buffer:** Forecasts are wrong, and being short costs far more than a little extra hardware, so planners add another month or two of growth.

**What it outputs:** A target for installed capacity at a future date. Combined with the lead time, that tells you when to place the order.

quiz.q: Same model, but growth jumps to 5 percent a month. Roughly how much capacity do you need installed in 6 months, before the buffer?
quiz.a: About 100 × 1.05^6 ≈ 134 PB used, so 134 / 0.8 ≈ 168 PB installed. Compounding plus the 80 percent fill target amplify the growth change.

mcq.q: In the basic capacity model, why divide projected usage by 0.8?
options: To keep the cluster at most 80 percent full
To convert raw bytes into replicated bytes
To account for 20 percent annual growth
To subtract disks expected to fail
mcq.why: The target maximum fill is 80 percent, leaving room for repair, rebalancing and bursts, so installed capacity is usage / 0.8.

predict.q: 100 PB used, 3% monthly growth, 6-month lead time, 80% max fill. Capacity needed at delivery?
options: About 149 PB
About 119 PB
About 180 PB

hook: Your cluster is 95% full and every disk is healthy. Why is that already a data-loss risk?
title: Never run distributed storage full: repair needs room
body: Distributed storage must never run full. When a disk or rack fails, its data must be re-created elsewhere from the remaining replicas or fragments, and that needs **free space** on other machines. At 95 percent full there may be no room to repair, so an ordinary failure becomes real data risk: the lost redundancy cannot be restored. That is why capacity models target a maximum fill like 80 percent.
takeaway: Free space is part of your durability, not wasted capacity.
deeper:
**The repair loop:** Replication and erasure coding protect data only if lost copies are rebuilt quickly. A full cluster breaks the loop: after a failure, data sits with reduced redundancy, and a second failure in that window can cause loss.

**Other jobs need room too:** Rebalancing needs space on destination servers. Continuous add-and-retire needs room to drain racks before power-off, since every chunk from a retiring rack must land elsewhere with full redundancy. Bursts of new data need space as well.

**A real operator's headroom:** Meta's representative 2021 Tectonic cluster held 1,250 PB of 1,590 PB, about 79 percent. It is also described as about 70 percent full, so the exact figure is uncertain, but either way it kept real headroom.

**Turn it into policy:** Decide which fill level triggers a hardware order and which triggers an incident, and plan capacity with lead time, growth, buffer and repair headroom.

quiz.q: A rack holding 2 PB fails in a cluster with 1.5 PB free. What's the danger, beyond the failure itself?
quiz.a: There isn't room to re-create the lost 2 PB of copies, so data stays under-protected; a second failure during that window could lose data.

mcq.q: Why must distributed storage keep free space even when nothing has failed?
options: Failed disks' data must be rebuilt somewhere
Writes slow down as disks approach full
Metadata needs 20 percent of raw capacity
Erasure coding stores parity in free space
mcq.why: When a disk or rack fails, its data is re-created on other machines; without free space, redundancy can't be restored.

predict.q: A cluster is 95% full and all disks are healthy. The biggest risk is:
options: No room to rebuild after the next failure
Writes getting slightly slower
The metadata service running out first

hook: Big fleets never do a big-bang hardware upgrade. So how do they swap out old racks every single week?
title: No big-bang upgrades: racks arrive and leave weekly
body: Big fleets never upgrade in one step: every week new racks arrive and old ones leave. That works only if three things hold. The placement layer supports **heterogeneous hardware**, like disks of different sizes weighted by capacity, as CRUSH weights do. New capacity is filled gradually through rate-limited rebalancing. And old capacity is drained before removal: mark the rack draining, move its data out, verify full redundancy elsewhere, then power off.
takeaway: Never unplug a rack the system still counts on.
deeper:
**Mixed generations are normal:** At any moment several generations of disks and servers coexist, with different capacities and speeds. Placement that assumes identical machines would overfill small disks and underuse big ones. Weighting, as in CRUSH's cluster map or vnode counts in consistent hashing, gives each device a share proportional to its capacity.

**Fill slowly:** An empty new rack attracts a flood of data from a naive balancer, which can saturate the network for hours. Rate limits keep that migration in the background.

**Drain safely:** Simply unplugging an old rack removes copies and cuts redundancy for every chunk it held, effectively simulating a large failure. Marking it draining stops new data landing there; data is copied out; the system verifies full redundancy for every chunk before anyone powers it off.

**The payoff:** Upgrades become routine background work instead of risky events.

quiz.q: A technician powers off a retiring rack as soon as its copy job reports 'done', skipping verification. Why is that risky?
quiz.a: If any chunk didn't fully re-replicate, powering off removes its copies like a rack failure would. Verify every chunk has full redundancy elsewhere first.

mcq.q: Why must placement support weighted, mixed hardware in a continuously upgraded fleet?
options: Several disk generations of different sizes coexist
Weights let placement ignore failure domains
New disks must hold all new data first
Old disks cannot be read once weighted
mcq.why: Racks arrive and retire weekly, so different disk sizes coexist; weighting by capacity, as CRUSH does, keeps each disk proportionally filled.

hook: Two fill levels matter more than any forecast. What are they, and how far apart must they be?
title: The gap between 'order hardware' and 'declare incident'
body: Capacity planning is where storage engineering meets finance. A useful review question: what fill level triggers a hardware order, and what fill level triggers an incident? The **gap** between them must be larger than the lead time multiplied by the worst realistic growth rate. If it is smaller, demand can reach the incident level before ordered hardware arrives, and the team is in crisis with nothing to deploy.
takeaway: Your runway must outlast your lead time at your worst growth, not your average.
deeper:
**Two thresholds, one runway:** The order threshold is when the team commits money. The incident threshold is the fill level where repair headroom is at risk and people get paged. Between them lies the runway.

**Size it for the bad month:** The runway must cover lead time times the worst realistic growth rate. In a simple model, 6 months at 3 percent monthly growth adds about 19 percent more data. If a launch or a new ML dataset could push growth faster, the gap must cover that rate, or a lumpy month eats the runway before new racks are installed and burned in.

**The finance trade:** A wider gap means buying earlier and carrying more idle hardware. A narrower gap saves money but risks running out.

**Write it down:** Both thresholds, tied to lead time and growth, let engineering and finance agree on the risk they take instead of discovering it during an outage.

quiz.q: Your order trigger is 70 percent full and your incident line is 80 percent. Lead time is 6 months and growth can hit 3 percent a month. Is the gap safe?
quiz.a: No. Six months at 3 percent adds about 19 percent more data, taking 70 percent to about 83 percent, past the incident line before hardware arrives. Order earlier.

mcq.q: The gap between order and incident fill levels must exceed what?
options: Lead time times the worst realistic growth rate
Lead time times the average growth rate
The raw capacity of a single rack
The data lost in one disk failure
mcq.why: If growth over the lead time can exceed the gap, the cluster hits the incident level before new hardware arrives.

hook: Each server is slow only 1 time in 100. Why can most of your users still hit the slow path?
title: Fan out to 100 servers and 63% of requests are slow
body: When one user request touches many servers, the slowest one decides the latency. Dean and Barroso's The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013) gives the classic example. A server usually answers in 10 ms, but 1 request in 100 takes 1 second. Touch one server and 1 in 100 user requests is slow. Wait on 100 in parallel and the chance all are fast is 0.99^100 ≈ 0.37, so about 63 percent take over a second.

stat.label: of requests slow at 100-way fan-out, 1% each

takeaway: At high fan-out, a rare per-server hiccup becomes the common user experience.
deeper:
**The math:** Each server independently has a 99 percent chance of being fast, so for N servers the chance all are fast is 0.99^N. At 100 that is about 37 percent. At 50, 1 - 0.99^50 ≈ 0.39, so about 39 percent of requests are slow.

**Where the tail comes from:** Background work such as compaction, scrubbing and rebalancing. Noisy neighbors in multi-tenant clusters. Queueing when requests arrive in bursts. Slowly failing hardware, like a disk that still works but responds slowly.

**Fan-out is everywhere:** Hash-partitioned range queries scatter to every shard. Salted counters read N sub-keys. Erasure-coded reads fetch many fragments. Each multiplies exposure to the tail.

**The catch:** You can't average your way out. The user waits for the maximum, not the mean, so tail techniques go after the slowest response directly.

quiz.q: A search query touches 50 index servers, each with a 1-in-100 chance of a 1-second stall. What fraction of queries stall, and what would you try first?
quiz.a: 1 - 0.99^50 ≈ 0.39, so about 39 percent. Try hedged requests after a p95 delay, and look for the root cause of the slow tail.

mcq.q: With 100-way fan-out and 1 percent slow servers, why are about 63 percent of requests slow?
options: All 100 are fast only 0.99^100 ≈ 37% of the time
Each server's slowness adds up to 100 percent
Parallel requests share one network queue
Slow servers retry and double the load
mcq.why: The user waits for all 100; the chance none is slow is 0.99^100 ≈ 0.37, so about 63 percent hit at least one slow server.

predict.q: Each server is slow 1% of the time. A request waits on 100 servers in parallel. Share of requests that are slow?
options: About 63 percent
About 1 percent
About 10 percent

hook: Google cut Bigtable's 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms. How much extra load did that cost?
title: Hedged requests: 1,800 ms to 74 ms for 2% more load
body: A **hedged request** goes to one replica first. If no reply arrives after a short delay, such as the 95th-percentile latency, a second copy goes to another replica, and the client uses whichever answers first. Most requests finish before the hedge fires, so extra load stays small. In a Google benchmark reading 1,000 keys from Bigtable across 100 servers, hedging after 10 ms cut p99.9 latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with only 2 percent more requests.

stat.label: extra requests to cut p99.9 from 1,800 to 74 ms

takeaway: Don't duplicate every request. Duplicate only the ones already running late.
deeper:
**The sequence:**
1. The client sends GET key to Replica A.
2. It waits about 10 ms, the p95 delay. No answer.
3. It sends a hedge GET key to Replica B.
4. Replica B returns the value quickly, and the client cancels the request to A.

**Why the delay makes it cheap:** Waiting until the 95th percentile means only the roughly 5 percent of requests already slow get hedged. Many of those are stuck behind a temporary problem on one replica, such as compaction or a noisy neighbor. A second replica is unlikely to be slow at the same moment, so the hedge usually wins.

**Still fix the cause:** Hedging after a p95 delay is the first thing to try for a fan-out tail, but keep looking for why the slow replicas are slow.

quiz.q: Your p50 is 5 ms, p95 is 12 ms, and p99.9 is 900 ms from occasional compaction stalls. When should a hedge fire, and why not at 1 ms?
quiz.a: Around 12 ms, the p95, so only the slowest ~5 percent get a second copy. Hedging at 1 ms would duplicate nearly every request and roughly double load.

mcq.q: In Google's Bigtable benchmark, what did hedging after 10 ms cost in extra requests?
options: About 2 percent more requests
About 50 percent more requests
About twice as many requests
About 10 percent more requests
mcq.why: Only requests still unanswered at 10 ms were hedged, so just 2 percent more requests cut p99.9 from 1,800 ms to 74 ms.

predict.q: Hedging after 10 ms cut Bigtable's p99.9 from 1,800 ms to 74 ms. Extra requests sent?
options: About 2 percent
About 50 percent
About 100 percent

hook: Send every request to two servers, yet do the work only once. How do the servers pull that off?
title: Tied requests: queue at two servers, execute at one
body: A hedge waits before sending its second copy, so a request stuck in a long queue still loses that time. A **tied request** goes to two servers at once, and each copy knows about the other. When one server actually starts executing, it tells the other to cancel. Whichever server reaches the request first does the work; the other drops it before spending effort. This attacks tail latency caused by **queueing**.
takeaway: Wait in two lines, get served in one, and let the other line forget you.
deeper:
**Why not just hedge:** Hedging adds a delay before the second copy exists. A tied request enqueues on both servers immediately, so it gets the shorter of the two queue waits with no delay.

**Cancellation keeps it cheap:** Without it, sending every request to two servers would double the load, which is exactly the problem with immediate hedging. Because the servers coordinate, only one normally does the work; the other copy is removed from its queue once execution starts elsewhere. Both might start at nearly the same moment, but that extra work is limited.

**Why queueing matters:** Requests arrive in bursts, and background work can occupy a server, so waiting behind others is a major source of the tail.

**The benefit:** The client gets whichever server happens to be less busy right now, without having to predict it.

quiz.q: Your slow requests spend 95 percent of their time waiting in server queues, not executing. Which fits better, hedged or tied requests, and why?
quiz.a: Tied requests. They enqueue on two servers immediately and cancel the loser when one starts executing, so you get the shorter queue without a hedge's upfront delay.

mcq.q: How do tied requests avoid doubling server work?
options: The server that starts executing cancels the other copy
The client cancels both copies after a timeout
Only one copy is sent unless the first fails
Both servers split the work in half
mcq.why: Each copy knows about the other; when one server begins executing, it tells the other to drop its queued copy.

hook: A read needs 10 fragments to rebuild the data. Why would you deliberately ask for 12?
title: Ask for 12 fragments, decode from the first 10
body: An RS(10,4) read that fetches exactly 10 fragments is as slow as the slowest of those 10 disks. **Erasure-code read slack** fixes that: since any 10 of the 14 fragments rebuild the data, request 11 or 12 and decode from the first 10 that arrive. Slow disks are simply ignored. A second tool attacks the cause: **separate background work**, scheduling compaction and repair below user traffic, as Tectonic's TrafficClasses do.
takeaway: Redundancy you bought for durability can also buy you speed.
deeper:
**Why slack works:** A plain RS(10,4) read is a fan-out of 10 with full exposure to the tail. Asking for one or two extra fragments means the read completes when the 10 fastest responses arrive. A disk that is busy, compacting or failing slowly is skipped automatically. The cost is modestly more read traffic.

**Why separate background work:** Compaction, scrubbing and rebalancing are named sources of the tail. Running them at the same priority as user traffic guarantees user requests sometimes queue behind them. Tectonic puts background work in Bronze, with lower-class requests yielding to Gold, so maintenance doesn't push up latency-sensitive traffic.

**The full toolkit:** Hedged requests, tied requests, read slack and deprioritized background work. At high fan-out the tail decides latency, and these cut it with small extra load.

quiz.q: One disk in an RS(10,4) group is failing slowly and takes 500 ms per read; the others take 10 ms. How does requesting 12 fragments change a typical read?
quiz.a: The read decodes from the first 10 fragments to arrive, so the slow disk's fragment is simply not needed; latency tracks the fast disks instead of the 500 ms one.

mcq.q: Why can an RS(10,4) reader decode from any 10 fragments it receives?
options: Any 10 of the 14 fragments can rebuild the data
Each fragment holds a full copy of the data
The 4 parity fragments are never needed
Fragments are replicated 10 times each
mcq.why: Reed-Solomon RS(10,4) tolerates losing any 4 of 14 fragments, so the first 10 to arrive are enough to decode.

hook: To kill tail latency, you send every request to two replicas at once. Why does the tail get worse?
title: Hedging immediately doubles load and lengthens the tail
body: A common mistake is hedging immediately, sending the duplicate at the same moment as the original. That doubles the load on storage, and more load means longer **queues**, which makes the tail you were fighting worse. The correct move: hedge only after a delay near the 95th-percentile latency, so only the slow few get a second copy, and **cap the hedge rate** so hedges cannot flood the system during a broad slowdown.
takeaway: A hedge is insurance for stragglers, not a second copy of everything.
deeper:
